### komando --help
exit 0
--- stdout
komando is one safe command line for
servers, databases, caches, queues, storage, clusters and VPNs,
for people and AI agents alike.

Start:
  komando host ssh add NAME USER@ADDRESS   add a server
  komando conn add NAME URL            add a database, cache, queue, storage,
                                       cluster or registry
  komando import ssh-config            bring in the servers you already have
  komando list                         see everything komando knows about
  komando test TARGET                  check that it answers and lets you in
  komando guide install                let your AI agent use komando safely

Targets: a server or service name, a pattern (web-*), @group, tag:NAME,
label:key=value, kind:KIND (host, db, cache, storage, postgres, ...),
os:windows or os:linux, all, or user@addr:port for a server you have not
added. Combine with commas; put ! in front to leave one out.
See them all with `komando list`.

Usage:
  komando [flags]
  komando [command]

Servers:
  cert         TLS certificates: when do they expire, and do they verify
  cp           Copy files, written SRC DST with TARGET:PATH (upload/download)
  cron         Cron entries on servers: see, set and remove them
  docker       Docker on servers: check, read logs, run compose, clean up
  download     Download files from servers or from file storage
  facts        System facts: OS and support, updates, Docker, open ports
  fs           Files on servers: read, edit, undo an edit, move, remove
  job          Long-running jobs on servers: start, follow, wait for, stop
  logs         Read logs from journald, a file or a container
  net          Network checks from servers: open ports, reachability, HTTP, DNS
  pkg          Packages on servers: install, update, remove, check for updates
  reboot       Reboot servers one at a time and check each came back
  recipe       Ready-made and saved commands: run them, save your own
  svc          Services on servers: check, start, stop, read logs
  sync         Copy a folder one way, sending only new and changed files
  upload       Upload a file to servers (many at once) or to file storage
  user         Linux user accounts: see, add, lock, remove

Data:
  cache        Caches (Redis, Valkey, memcached): read and change keys
  db           Databases: query safely, look at the schema, back up, restore
  queue        Queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SQS, Pub/Sub): read, send, manage
  storage      Buckets (S3, GCS, Azure) and file servers: browse, copy, remove

Platform:
  cluster      Kubernetes and Docker Swarm: check, read logs, roll out, scale
  registry     Container registries: see images, copy them, clean up

Inventory:
  conn         Conns (databases, caches, queues, ...): add, change, remove
  export       Save servers, conns, VPNs, recipes and settings to a file
  group        Groups of servers, conns and VPNs: see and change who is in them
  host         Servers in komando's list: add, change, check, remove
  import       Bring in what you have: ssh config, .pgpass, my.cnf, .env
  rename       Rename one entry, or all names starting with OLD (--starts-with)

Access:
  key          SSH keys: make, add, put on servers, take off
  secret       Saved passwords and tokens: store, check, use as secret:NAME
  vpn          VPNs komando connects when a path needs one: add, connect, check

Overview:
  audit        Show the audit log: who did what, where, and the result
  doctor       Check komando's setup, your list and its security
  list         List servers, conns and VPNs
  status       What komando left running: VPNs, logins, tunnels, jobs
  test         Check that servers, conns and VPNs answer and let you in

Setup:
  completion   Print a tab-completion script for your shell
  config       Settings: read and change timeouts, host keys, the audit
  guide        The rules for AI agents, and how komando works (read first)
  help         Show the help of a command
  policy       Rules that block destructive commands: see, test, add, remove
  schema       Every command, flag and exit code, machine-readable
  ssh-gate     Let an SSH key run komando here and nothing else (person only)
  update       Update komando to the newest release
  version      Print the komando version and its home folder

Flags:
      --connect-timeout duration   time to connect, like 30s (default: setting connect_timeout, 15s)
      --dry-run[=true|false]       show what would run, changing nothing
  -h, --help[=true|false]          help for komando
      --host-key-policy string     accept-new, strict or off: how a server's key is checked (default: setting host_key_policy, accept-new)
      --max-output bytes           bytes kept per stream per server, like 1MiB (default: setting max_output_bytes, 256KiB)
  -o, --output string              json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                                   text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                                   takes csv and tsv
  -P, --parallel int               servers at once (default: setting parallel, 10)
      --pretty[=true|false]        indent JSON output
      --timeout duration           time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -v, --version[=true|false]       version for komando

Safety overrides (ask a person first):
      --allow-dangerous[=true|false]   run a command the safety rules would block
      --reveal[=true|false]            show passwords and keys in output (an agent needs a person's yes)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]               confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Additional help topics:
  komando environment  The environment variables komando reads
  komando exit-codes   What komando's exit codes mean
  komando output       Text for people, JSON for programs
  komando safety       How komando keeps a change from going wrong

Use "komando [command] --help" for more information about a command.

For scripts and AI agents:
  When piped, every command prints one JSON envelope on stdout; in a terminal
  it prints text (force it with -o json or -o text):
    {"ok":true,"command":"exec","data":{...},"meta":{...}}
    {"ok":false,"command":"exec","error":{"code":"AUTH_FAILED",...}}
  Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 usage, 3 not found, 4 connect or login,
              5 failed on the server, 6 blocked for safety, 7 timeout,
              8 precondition or conflict.
  komando guide is the playbook for agents; komando schema lists every command.
--- stderr
### komando audit --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Every change komando makes, and every blocked attempt, is a sealed record in
~/.komando/store.db: when, who (and which AI agent), the command, its
targets and whether it worked. The newest entries come last.

--since and --until take how long ago (30m, 12h, 7d), today, yesterday,
or a time (2026-11-07, '2026-11-07 14:30', 2026-11-07T14:30:00Z); a time
without a zone is this computer's. --since keeps entries from that moment
on, --until those before it. With either, every match is shown unless -n
is given.

Usage:
  komando audit [flags]
  komando audit [command]

Examples:
  komando audit                      # the last 50
  komando audit -n 0 --target @prod  # everything about @prod
  komando audit --command host. --failed
  komando audit --since 2h           # everything in the last two hours
  komando audit --since yesterday --until today --target @prod
  komando audit --actor claude --since 7d        # what Claude Code did this week
  komando audit verify               # was the log changed outside komando?

Available Commands:
  verify      Check that no audit record was changed, added or removed outside komando

Flags:
      --actor string          only what this one did: part of the name in KOMANDO_ACTOR, the AI agent (claude, codex ...) or the computer account
      --command string        only commands that start with this (like exec, svc.)
      --failed[=true|false]   only actions that failed or were blocked
  -h, --help[=true|false]     help for audit
  -n, --limit int             the newest N entries (0 = all; with --since or --until, all unless given) (default 50)
      --since string          only entries from this time on: 2h, 7d, today, 2026-11-07 or '2026-11-07 14:30'
      --target string         only entries for these servers or conns (a selector, like @prod)
      --until string          only entries before this time (the same forms as --since)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando audit [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

### komando cache --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Read and change keys in Redis, Valkey or memcached. Add a cache with
`komando cache redis add`.

get, keys and info only read. set changes data (a protected cache asks
first); rm deletes keys, so it also needs --allow-dangerous. `cache redis
raw` sends any command, but only reads unless --write; commands that flush,
block, run scripts or reconfigure the server also need --allow-dangerous.

Usage:
  komando cache [flags]
  komando cache [command]

Aliases:
  cache, redis, caches

Examples:
  komando cache redis add prod-redis redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1 --ask-password
  komando cache info prod-redis
  komando cache keys prod-redis 'session:*'
  komando cache get prod-redis session:42
  komando cache set prod-redis maintenance on --ttl 30m --dry-run

Available Commands:
  get         Show a key: its type, time to live and value (any type)
  info        Server summary: version, role, memory, clients, keys, hit rate
  keys        List keys matching a pattern (uses SCAN, so a big cache is not blocked)
  memcached   Memcached caches: save them, and send them a command
  redis       Redis caches: save them, and send them a command
  rm          Delete keys by exact name, never by pattern
  set         Set a string key, replacing any old value

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for cache

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando cache [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

### komando cache info --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Without arguments, a short summary: version, role, uptime, memory use and
limit, eviction policy, clients, keys per database and the hit rate. A
SECTION (server, clients, memory, persistence, stats, replication, cpu,
commandstats, keyspace, ...) or --all shows the raw INFO fields.

Usage:
  komando cache info CONN [SECTION] [flags]

Examples:
  komando cache info prod-redis
  komando cache info prod-redis memory
  komando cache info prod-redis --all

Flags:
  -a, --all[=true|false]    every field of the default INFO sections
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for info

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cache memcached --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Memcached caches: save them, and send them a command

Usage:
  komando cache memcached [flags]
  komando cache memcached [command]

Examples:
  komando cache memcached add prod-mc memcached://cache.internal:11211 --via web1 --dry-run
  komando cache memcached add prod-mc memcached://cache.internal:11211 --via web1
  komando cache memcached test prod-mc
  komando cache memcached raw prod-mc -- stats
  komando cache memcached raw prod-mc --write -- flush_all --dry-run

Available Commands:
  add         Save a memcached cache under a short name
  edit        Change a saved memcached cache (only the flags you pass change)
  list        List the saved memcached caches
  raw         Send one memcached command and show the reply
  remove      Forget a saved memcached cache (the cache is not touched)
  rename      Rename a saved memcached cache and every reference to it
  show        Show a saved memcached cache's settings (credentials as names)
  test        Check that a saved memcached cache answers and lets you in

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for memcached

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando cache memcached [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando cache memcached add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Save a memcached cache under a short name.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando cache memcached add NAME [URL] [flags]

Examples:
  komando cache memcached add app memcached://cache.internal:11211 --via web1
  komando cache memcached add app memcached://cache.internal:11211 --dry-run

Flags:
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored as a password credential
      --credential string           what it logs in with
      --group strings               put it in these groups
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --login string                how the password is used: ask at every connect, a stored one, or none
      --notes string                free-form notes, shown to people and agents
      --option stringArray          an option of this provider, KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace an entry that has the same name
      --protected[=true|false]      changes need a person's yes
      --tag strings                 tags, like prod
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cache memcached edit --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Change a saved memcached cache (only the flags you pass change).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando cache memcached edit NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando cache memcached edit app --add-tag critical
  komando cache memcached edit app --notes 'main one' --dry-run

Flags:
      --add-group strings           put it in these groups
      --add-tag strings             add these tags
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored as a password credential
      --credential string           what it logs in with
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for edit
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --login string                how the password is used: ask at every connect, a stored one, or none
      --notes string                free-form notes, shown to people and agents
      --option stringArray          an option of this provider, KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --protected[=true|false]      changes need a person's yes
      --rm-group strings            take it out of these groups
      --rm-tag strings              remove these tags
      --unset strings               clear these settings: via, credential, notes, protected
      --url string                  the new URL (the provider may not change)
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cache memcached raw --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Send one memcached command and show the reply.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the cache command
deletes data (DEL, FLUSHALL, ...): dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person
types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous.

Usage:
  komando cache memcached raw NAME -- COMMAND... [flags]

Examples:
  komando cache memcached raw app -- stats
  komando cache memcached raw app --write -- flush_all --dry-run
  komando cache memcached raw app --write -- flush_all --dry-run

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for raw
      --write[=true|false]   allow a command that changes data (it only reads without this)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando cache redis --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Redis caches: save them, and send them a command

Usage:
  komando cache redis [flags]
  komando cache redis [command]

Examples:
  komando cache redis add prod-redis redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1 --dry-run
  komando cache redis add prod-redis redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1
  komando cache redis test prod-redis
  komando cache redis raw prod-redis -- HGETALL user:42
  komando cache redis raw prod-redis --write -- EXPIRE session:42 3600 --dry-run

Available Commands:
  add         Save a redis cache under a short name
  edit        Change a saved redis cache (only the flags you pass change)
  list        List the saved redis caches
  raw         Send one redis command and show the reply
  remove      Forget a saved redis cache (the cache is not touched)
  rename      Rename a saved redis cache and every reference to it
  show        Show a saved redis cache's settings (credentials as names)
  test        Check that a saved redis cache answers and lets you in

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for redis

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cert check --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Reads certificates and says when they expire. It only reads.

A server (or @group, tag:, ...): komando looks for the certificates the
server uses: certbot's /etc/letsencrypt/live/*/cert.pem and the files that
nginx (ssl_certificate), haproxy (crt) and apache (SSLCertificateFile) name,
plus any --path. Files that need root are read with sudo only when sudo
works without a password; komando never asks for one. Only the CERTIFICATE
blocks of a file leave the server: a private key in the same file never
does. When certbot is there, the state of its renewal timer is shown too.

A website (https://example.com, example.com:443) or a conn that uses TLS:
komando connects from this computer (or through --via, or the conn's own
--via), reads the certificate the server sends and checks that it is
trusted and matches the name.

A certificate that expires within --warn (default 30d), has expired, is not
trusted, or a certbot renewal that failed is a problem: the command then
exits 1 (code CERT_PROBLEMS), like `komando doctor`.

Usage:
  komando cert check TARGET|URL... [flags]

Examples:
  komando cert check web1
  komando cert check @prod --warn 14d
  komando cert check https://shop.example.com api.example.com:8443
  komando cert check https://intranet.local --via bastion
  komando cert check web1 --path /etc/ssl/private/site.pem

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for check
      --path strings        also check this certificate file (or folder) on the servers
      --via string          reach websites through this server or VPN (a --via path)
      --warn duration       flag certificates that expire within this time (like 30d, 72h) (default 30d)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando cluster --help
exit 0
--- stdout
TARGET is a Kubernetes cluster (bring yours in with `komando import
kubeconfig`) or a Swarm manager server. The same verbs work on both. Reads
need nothing; restart, scale and apply change the cluster (protected targets
need --yes; try --dry-run); rm needs --allow-dangerous. Anything else:
`cluster run` passes the native kubectl or docker command, read-only unless
--write.

A cluster's usual namespace is its kubeconfig context's; change it with
`komando conn edit NAME --option namespace=shop`, or name one per command
with --namespace.

Usage:
  komando cluster [flags]
  komando cluster [command]

Aliases:
  cluster, k8s, kube, swarm, clusters

Examples:
  komando import kubeconfig                       # one cluster per kubeconfig context
  komando cluster status prod-k8s                     # version, nodes, what is not healthy
  komando cluster list prod-k8s pods --namespace shop
  komando cluster logs prod-k8s deploy/api --namespace shop -f
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deploy/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait

Available Commands:
  add         Add a cluster
  apply       Apply Kubernetes YAML or deploy a Swarm stack
  deploy      Roll out a new image
  describe    One object in short: state, images, conditions, pods, events
  events      Recent events, oldest first (--warnings for problems only)
  exec        Run a command in a pod, checked by the policy
  forward     Reach a pod or service port from this computer (127.0.0.1) until Ctrl-C
  get         Show one object in full, Secret values hidden
  helm        Helm releases, read only: see their state, history and values
  history     Revisions of a deployment, newest first, with their images
  list        List pods, deployments, services, nodes ... (Swarm: services, tasks)
  logs        Logs of a pod, a workload, a label (-l) or a Swarm service
  restart     Restart a workload with a rolling restart, or a Swarm service
  rm          Delete an object, service or stack
  rollback    Go back to an earlier version of a workload
  run         Run any kubectl or docker command (read only by default)
  scale       Set the number of replicas
  shell       Open a shell in a pod, like kubectl exec (person only)
  status      Show the version, the nodes and what is not healthy

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for cluster

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando cluster [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando cluster add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Same as `komando conn add NAME URL`, for a cluster.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Saves a cluster under a short name. Typed alone at a terminal, it asks
step by step. The URL scheme sets the kind: `komando conn kinds` lists them.

A Kubernetes cluster usually comes in with `komando import kubeconfig FILE`
(one conn per context). Here its kubeconfig must be in the vault already
(--password-ref). A Docker Swarm manager is a server: `komando host ssh
add`.

Usage:
  komando cluster add NAME URL [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster add prod-k8s k8s://api.cluster.example:6443 --password-ref secret:prod-kubeconfig
  komando cluster add prod-k8s k8s://api.cluster.example:6443 --password-ref secret:prod-kubeconfig --dry-run

Flags:
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored in the vault as secret:NAME-pass and used as --password-ref
  -g, --group strings               put it in these groups (comma-separated)
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --login string                how komando logs in, as show names it: ask (a person types the password at every connect; never stored), password (a stored one: with --ask-password or --password-ref); a server also takes key (with --key or --identity) and agent (ssh-agent and ~/.ssh only), a conn none (no password of komando's own)
      --notes string                free-form notes (komando conn show shows them to people and agents)
      --option stringArray          an option of this kind, KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace a conn that has the same name
      --password-ref string         where the password is: secret:NAME (saved with komando secret set NAME), env:VAR, file:PATH or a password manager like op://...
      --protected[=true|false]      production: komando asks you before every change, and an AI agent needs your yes in a window
  -t, --tag strings                 tags, like prod (comma-separated)
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cluster apply --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Kubernetes: applies every object in FILE server-side and says per object
whether it was created, configured or unchanged. --dry-run asks the server
what would change and shows it as a diff (Secret values stay hidden; a
changed value shows as "[hidden, changed]"). Objects without a namespace go
to --namespace; one that names another namespace is refused.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

A field another field manager owns (an autoscaler's replicas, a kubectl
edit) stops the apply with K8S_CONFLICT naming that manager, and nothing
is applied. --force-conflicts takes those fields over, as
`kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts` does.

Swarm: deploys FILE (a compose file) as the stack --stack; --dry-run checks
the file with `docker stack config` on the manager.

Usage:
  komando cluster apply TARGET --file FILE [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster apply prod-k8s --file app.yaml --dry-run
  komando cluster apply prod-k8s --file app.yaml
  komando cluster apply swarm1 --file compose.yml --stack shop

Flags:
  -f, --file string                    YAML file ('-' for stdin)
      --force-conflicts[=true|false]   Kubernetes: take over fields another field manager owns
  -h, --help[=true|false]              help for apply
  -n, --namespace string               Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)
      --stack string                   Swarm: the stack name

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando cluster deploy --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Sets the image of a deployment, statefulset or daemonset (Kubernetes) or a
service (Swarm). With several containers, name one with --container (or
write --image NAME=IMAGE). --wait stays until every replica runs the new
image, the rollout fails, or --timeout (default 5m) passes; go back with
`komando cluster rollback`.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando cluster deploy TARGET TYPE/NAME --image IMAGE [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deployment/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait
  komando cluster deploy prod-k8s deployment/api --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 --namespace shop --wait --dry-run
  komando cluster deploy swarm1 service/web --image nginx:1.27 --wait

Flags:
  -c, --container string    which container gets the image (needed when there are several)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for deploy
      --image string        the new image, like ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.3 (or CONTAINER=IMAGE)
  -n, --namespace string    Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)
      --wait[=true|false]   wait until the rollout finishes (or fails; --timeout, default 5m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cluster exec --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Runs COMMAND in the pod (for TYPE/NAME, in one of its pods) and returns its
output. Commands that only look can say so with --read-only: it runs only
commands komando knows only read (cat, ls, printenv ...) and refuses any
other; a protected cluster then needs no --yes. For an
interactive shell use `komando cluster shell TARGET POD`.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando cluster exec TARGET POD|TYPE/NAME -- COMMAND... [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster exec prod-k8s deploy/api --namespace shop --read-only -- cat /app/config.yml
  komando cluster exec prod-k8s api-7d9f-x2 -c api --namespace shop -- php artisan cache:clear

Flags:
  -c, --container string         container in the pod
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for exec
  -n, --namespace string         Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)
      --read-only[=true|false]   declare that the command only looks: only commands komando knows only read run (protected clusters: no --yes)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando cluster forward --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Forwards 127.0.0.1:LOCAL on this computer to REMOTE on a pod, deployment or
service, through the conn's --via path. It runs until Ctrl-C (or --timeout).
Only this computer can use it. For a service, REMOTE is the service's port;
komando forwards to the pod's port behind it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando cluster forward TARGET TYPE/NAME [LOCAL:]REMOTE [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster forward prod-k8s svc/api 8080:80 --namespace shop
  komando cluster forward prod-k8s svc/api 8080:80 --namespace shop --dry-run
  komando cluster forward prod-k8s deploy/db 15432:5432 --namespace shop
  komando cluster forward prod-k8s svc/api :80 --namespace shop   # any free local port

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for forward
  -n, --namespace string    Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cluster logs --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Name a pod, a workload (deploy/api, statefulset/db, svc/web: all its pods)
or pick pods by label with -l. Lines from several pods start with [pod]. -f
keeps reading until Ctrl-C or --timeout (both end it normally); it follows
the pods that exist when it starts. --since takes a duration back from now
(10m, 2h) or a time (2026-01-02T10:00:00Z).

Usage:
  komando cluster logs TARGET [POD|TYPE/NAME] [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster logs prod-k8s api-7d9f-x2 --namespace shop --since 10m
  komando cluster logs prod-k8s deploy/api --namespace shop -f
  komando cluster logs prod-k8s -l app=api --namespace shop --limit 50
  komando cluster logs swarm1 service/web -f

Flags:
  -c, --container string          container in the pod
  -f, --follow[=true|false]       keep reading new lines (Ctrl-C or --timeout stops)
  -h, --help[=true|false]         help for logs
      --limit int                 the most lines per pod (the last ones) (default 200)
  -n, --namespace string          Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)
      --previous[=true|false]     the previous run of a restarted container
  -l, --selector string           read every pod with these labels, like app=api
      --since string              only newer than this: 10m, 2h, or a time like 2026-01-02T10:00:00Z
      --timestamps[=true|false]   start each line with its time

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cluster rollback --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Without --revision, a deployment goes back to the newest earlier revision
that runs other images than now. After a rollback, the revision it replaced
(the broken one) is skipped, so a second rollback does not bring it back;
--revision picks any revision. A Swarm service goes back to its previous
version.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando cluster rollback TARGET TYPE/NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster rollback prod-k8s deployment/api --namespace shop --wait
  komando cluster rollback prod-k8s deployment/api --namespace shop --wait --dry-run
  komando cluster rollback prod-k8s deployment/api --revision 3 --namespace shop
  komando cluster rollback swarm1 service/web

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for rollback
  -n, --namespace string    Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)
      --revision int        the revision to go back to (default: the previous one with other images)
      --wait[=true|false]   wait until the rollback finishes (--timeout, default 5m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando cluster run --help
exit 0
--- stdout
For Kubernetes, komando runs the kubectl command itself (no kubectl
needed) and reaches the API through the conn's --via path: get (tables,
wide, name, json, yaml, jsonpath, custom-columns, -w), describe, logs,
events, top, explain, version, api-resources, api-versions, cluster-info,
auth can-i/whoami, wait, rollout, apply, diff, create, replace, delete,
patch, label, annotate, scale, set image, cordon, uncordon, drain, taint,
run, exec, cp, debug, certificate and config. For Swarm, docker runs on the
manager. Commands that change things need --write; delete, drain and other
risky verbs also need --allow-dangerous.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the cluster command
deletes something or scales to 0: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person
types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as
well.

Usage:
  komando cluster run TARGET -- ARGS... [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster run prod-k8s -- get pods -A -o wide
  komando cluster run prod-k8s --write -- rollout undo deployment/api -n shop
  komando cluster run prod-k8s --write --dry-run -- rollout undo deployment/api -n shop
  komando cluster run swarm1 -- service ps web

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for run
      --write[=true|false]   allow commands that change the cluster

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando cluster status --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Without an object: the version, the nodes, and every problem (pods that do
not run, workloads short of replicas, nodes that are not ready; on Swarm,
services short of replicas with their tasks' errors). --namespace limits it
to one namespace. A selector that picks several clusters (@prod, kind:k8s)
shows each in data.results.

With TYPE/NAME (or TYPE NAME) on one cluster: whether that workload has
rolled out. --wait stays until it has, it fails, or --timeout (default 5m)
passes.

Usage:
  komando cluster status TARGET [TYPE/NAME] [flags]

Examples:
  komando cluster status prod-k8s
  komando cluster status @prod                  # every cluster in the group, at once
  komando cluster status prod-k8s deployment/api --namespace shop --wait
  komando cluster status swarm1 service/web --wait

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for status
  -n, --namespace string    Kubernetes namespace (default: the context's, else default)
      --wait[=true|false]   with TYPE/NAME: wait until it has rolled out (--timeout, default 5m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)

### komando completion bash --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Prints the tab-completion script for bash. Turn it on once, then open a new
terminal:

  echo 'eval "$(komando completion bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc

On macOS, where a new terminal reads ~/.bash_profile, add the line there.
Completing flags and names works without the bash-completion package; with
it, bash completes a little more.

Usage:
  komando completion bash

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]              help for bash
      --no-descriptions[=true|false]   disable completion descriptions

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv

Sets up a one-time code (TOTP, like a bank or GitHub login) for komando's
"Allow once" window: once on, allowing an AI agent's --yes,
--allow-dangerous or --reveal needs the 6-digit code from the authenticator

stays set for Linux, BSD and Windows on the same vault. Only a person at a

### komando config set --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Settings:
  host_key_policy  accept-new | strict | off
      how server identity is checked: accept-new pins a new server's key, strict needs `host ssh trust` first, off checks nothing (needs --yes)
  default_user     a login name
      user for servers that have none (empty: your own user name)
  default_timeout  duration > 0
      how long a remote command may run (--timeout overrides it)
  connect_timeout  duration > 0
      how long connecting may take (--connect-timeout overrides it)
  parallel         1 or more
      how many servers a command works on at once (-P overrides it)
  max_output_bytes 1024 or more
      output kept per stream and server, in bytes (--max-output overrides it)
  audit            on | off
      keep the audit log (turning it off needs --yes)
  audit_sql        full | hash | off
      how SQL text is kept in the audit log: hash keeps a SHA-256 so repeated queries can be matched (off needs --yes)
  audit_syslog     udp://HOST:514 | tcp://HOST:514 | tls://HOST:6514 | off
      also send each audit record to a log server (syslog, RFC 5424); changing it needs --yes
  mask_personal    protected | all | off
      where AI agents see email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers and IBANs hidden: on protected servers and conns (the default), on all, or nowhere (less needs --yes)
  login_for        duration
      how long `komando login SERVER` keeps a server's login for later commands (an AI agent's too)
  approval_languageauto | en | id
      the language of the approval window: auto follows the system language (Indonesian when it is id, else English)
  vpn_idle         duration, 0 = never
      a VPN kept up with `vpn up` is closed after this long unused

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the setting turns a
check off: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

To go back to a default, set the value from the DEFAULT column of `komando
config show`.

Usage:
  komando config set SETTING VALUE [flags]

Examples:
  komando config set parallel 20
  komando config set parallel 20 --dry-run
  komando config set default_timeout 10m
  komando config set host_key_policy strict
  komando config set audit_sql hash

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for set

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando conn --help
exit 0
--- stdout
A conn is a database, cache, message queue, file storage, cluster or
registry komando talks to directly. The kind comes from the URL scheme
(`komando conn kinds` lists them). Passwords never go in the URL: store them
with `komando secret set` and pass --password-ref. Use --via HOST when the
conn is only reachable from a server.

Conns share names and selectors (@group, tag:x, glob, all) with servers.

Usage:
  komando conn [flags]
  komando conn [command]

Aliases:
  conn, conns

Examples:
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.9/shop --password-ref secret:prod-db-pass
  komando test prod-db                              # does it answer and let komando in?
  komando conn edit prod-db --via web1 --dry-run
  komando conn rm prod-db                           # from komando only

Available Commands:
  add         Add a conn (the URL scheme sets its kind)
  edit        Change a conn (only the flags you pass change)
  kinds       List the conn kinds komando knows and their URL schemes
  list        List conns
  rename      Rename a conn and every reference to it
  rm          Remove conns (from komando only)
  show        Show all settings of a conn (secrets as references, never values)
  test        Check that conns answer and let you in

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for conn

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando conn [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando conn add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Add a conn (the URL scheme sets its kind).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando conn add NAME URL [flags]

Examples:
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5:5432/app --via web1 --password-ref secret:prod-db-pass --protected
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5:5432/app --via web1 --password-ref secret:prod-db-pass --protected --dry-run
  komando conn add shop mysql://shop@db.internal/shop --group shop
  komando conn add local sqlite:///var/lib/app.db
  komando conn add cache redis://default@10.0.0.7:6379/0 --via web1 --password-ref secret:redis-pass
  komando conn add backups 's3://AKIAEXAMPLE@my-bucket/db?region=eu-west-1' --password-ref secret:s3-secret
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5/app --via web1 --ask-password   # type it now (hidden)
  komando conn add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5/app --via web1 --login ask      # type it at every connect; never stored

Flags:
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored in the vault as secret:NAME-pass and used as --password-ref
  -g, --group strings               put it in these groups (comma-separated)
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --login string                how komando logs in, as show names it: ask (a person types the password at every connect; never stored), password (a stored one: with --ask-password or --password-ref); a server also takes key (with --key or --identity) and agent (ssh-agent and ~/.ssh only), a conn none (no password of komando's own)
      --notes string                free-form notes (komando conn show shows them to people and agents)
      --option stringArray          an option of this kind, KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace a conn that has the same name
      --password-ref string         where the password is: secret:NAME (saved with komando secret set NAME), env:VAR, file:PATH or a password manager like op://...
      --protected[=true|false]      production: komando asks you before every change, and an AI agent needs your yes in a window
  -t, --tag strings                 tags, like prod (comma-separated)
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

Change a conn (only the flags you pass change).

      --option stringArray          set an option of this kind, KEY=VALUE (an empty value removes it) (default [])

      --protected[=true|false]      production: komando asks you before every change, and an AI agent needs your yes in a window
      --rm-group strings            take it out of these groups
      --rm-tag strings              remove these tags
      --unset strings               clear these settings: via,password-ref,notes,protected
      --url string                  new URL (the kind may change with the scheme)
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing

### komando cp --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Remote paths are written TARGET:PATH (TARGET: alone, or TARGET:~/x, is the
login user's home folder). Uploads accept any target selector (@group,
tag:x, ...) and run in parallel. Downloads from several servers go to
DST/<server>/... . A single-file copy reports its sha256, so you can check
it. TARGET can be a storage conn too (backups:2026/db.sql.gz). cp is upload
or download written the cp way: the same code, flags and results.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

With TARGET:PATH on both sides, cp copies from one server or storage conn
to another (server to server, storage to storage, or one of each). The
data streams through this computer and is never saved on its disk. The
file at the destination is replaced, as an upload replaces it.

--continue goes on with a single file that was cut off: the part already
at the destination is kept when it matches the source (sha256), the rest
is sent, and the whole file is checked against the source. A destination
that is longer, or differs, stops with RESUME_CONFLICT and is not touched.
S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob and WebDAV store a file whole and
cannot add to one (RESUME_UNSUPPORTED).

Folders (-r), like cp and rsync:
  SRC/  (trailing slash)  the contents of SRC go into DST
  SRC   into a new DST    DST becomes the copy of SRC
  SRC   into a folder DST of the same name (site -> /var/www/site): DST is
        updated in place, so running the same copy again never nests site/site
  SRC   into another existing folder DST: the copy is DST/SRC
Symbolic links are not copied (they are listed as skipped). For repeatable
deploys that send only changed files, use `komando sync`.

Usage:
  komando cp SRC DST [flags]

Aliases:
  cp, copy

Examples:
  komando cp ./app.tar.gz @web:/tmp/app.tar.gz
  komando cp -r ./site web1:/var/www/site
  komando cp ./nginx.conf web1:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf --sudo
  komando cp web1:/var/log/nginx/error.log ./logs/
  komando cp @web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./configs/
  komando cp ./db.sql.gz backups:2026/db.sql.gz
  komando cp web1:/var/backups/db.sql.gz web2:/var/backups/
  komando cp -r web1:/var/www/site backups:sites/
  komando cp web1:/var/backups/db.sql.gz ./db.sql.gz --continue

Flags:
      --continue[=true|false]    go on with a copy that was cut off: keep the part already at the destination when it matches the source, send the rest, then check the whole file (sha256)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for cp
      --mode string              upload: file mode, like 0755
      --overwrite[=true|false]   download: replace files that already exist on this computer
  -p, --parents[=true|false]     upload: create missing parent folders
      --progress[=true|false]    with -o json, write progress to the error output (stderr), one JSON object per line
  -r, --recursive[=true|false]   copy folders (a trailing / on SRC copies its contents)
      --size bytes               an upload from stdin (-): how many bytes it sends, like 10MiB; a stream of another length replaces nothing (SIZE_CONFLICT)
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        single files with sudo: install as root (upload), read as root (download)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)

### komando cron --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Cron runs commands on a schedule (every night at 2, every 5 minutes ...).
komando manages crontab entries by NAME: each is tagged with '#
komando:<name>', so 'cron set' replaces the entry with the same NAME instead
of adding a second one, and 'cron rm' removes only that entry. Other lines
of the crontab are kept as they are.

Usage:
  komando cron [flags]
  komando cron [command]

Aliases:
  cron, crons

Examples:
  komando cron list web1
  komando cron set web1 nightly-backup '/usr/local/bin/backup.sh' --schedule '0 2 * * *'
  komando cron rm web1 nightly-backup

Available Commands:
  list        Show crontab entries
  rm          Remove the cron entry with this NAME
  set         Create or replace the entry with this NAME

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for cron
      --user string         crontab of this user (uses sudo)

      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando cron [command] --help" for more information about a command.

### komando db --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Look at and query your databases. Add one with `komando db add`.

Without --write every query runs in a read-only transaction (SQL Server: one
that is always rolled back), so nothing can change. With --write, try
--dry-run first: it runs the SQL and rolls it back, showing how many rows
would change.

Each database is a conn: list them with `komando list kind:db`, check one
with `komando test TARGET`, change it with `komando conn edit NAME`, rename
it with `komando conn rename OLD NEW` and remove it with `komando conn rm
TARGET`.

Usage:
  komando db [flags]
  komando db [command]

Aliases:
  db, sql, dbs, database, databases

Examples:
  komando db add prod-db postgres://app@10.0.0.5:5432/shop --password-ref secret:shop-pw
  komando db query prod-db "select id, email from users order by id desc limit 10"
  komando db schema prod-db users
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod.sql.gz
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod.sql.gz --dry-run

Available Commands:
  activity    Sessions running something now: pid, user, how long, what
  add         Add a database
  dump        Save a copy of a database to a file on this computer (person only)
  explain     Show how the database would run a query (--analyze runs it and measures)
  grant       Give a user privileges on a database, schema or table (or a role)
  info        Show the version, size, connections and the replica role
  kill        Stop a session's running query (--session ends the connection)
  locks       Sessions waiting for a lock, and the session that holds it
  query       Run SQL (read only by default)
  restore     Load a backup into a database
  revoke      Take privileges (or a role) away from a user
  schema      List tables, or show columns and indexes of the named tables
  shell       Open an SQL shell, read only by default (person only)
  sizes       Databases, and the biggest tables and indexes
  user        Database users: see, add, change passwords, remove

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for db

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando db [command] --help" for more information about a command.

### komando db dump --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Saves a copy of the database to a file on this computer. Without --to the
file is CONN-<date>.sql.gz (SQLite: CONN-<date>.db) in this
folder. A file ending in .gz is compressed. Afterwards komando prints the
command that loads it back.

Safety: it only reads; when an AI agent runs it (the file holds every row,
secrets included): only a person at a terminal can run it; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

pg_dump or mysqldump runs on a server that has it: the one you name with
--run-on HOST, else the database's --via server. It connects to the conn
URL's address from that server, runs at low priority (nice, ionice) and
streams the backup back over SSH. Without such a server (a direct connection
or a VPN) komando writes plain SQL itself. PostgreSQL can also write its own
archive with --format custom (compressed, restored with pg_restore; needs
pg_dump on a server). --table and --schema-only narrow the dump. SQLite
databases are copied as a database file instead. An existing FILE is never
overwritten. The file holds your data: it is created readable only by you.

Usage:
  komando db dump CONN [flags]

Examples:
  komando db dump prod-db                  # saves prod-db-<date>.sql.gz here
  komando db dump prod-db --to backups/    # the same name, inside backups/
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod-2026-11-02.sql.gz
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod.dump --format custom
  komando db dump prod-db --to prod.dump --format custom --run-on db1
  komando db dump prod-db --to orders.sql --table public.orders --table public.order_items
  komando db dump prod-db --to schema.sql --schema-only
  komando db dump local --to backup.db

Flags:
      --format string              plain (SQL) or custom (PostgreSQL archive for pg_restore) (default "plain")
  -h, --help[=true|false]          help for dump
      --run-on string              run pg_dump or mysqldump on this server (default: the database's --via server)
      --schema-only[=true|false]   tables, indexes and functions, no rows
      --table stringArray          only this table (repeatable; SCHEMA.TABLE on PostgreSQL)
      --to string                  file to create on this computer (default: CONN-<date>.sql.gz; SQLite: CONN-<date>.db)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando db grant --help
exit 0
--- stdout
OBJECT for PostgreSQL: database:NAME, schema:NAME, table:[SCHEMA.]TABLE or
all-tables:SCHEMA; --role ROLE makes the user a member of ROLE. For MySQL:
DB.*, DB.TABLE or *.* (with --from-host for the account host). For
ClickHouse: DB.*, DB.TABLE or *.*, or database:DB, table:DB.TABLE.
Snowflake: not available (db user show reads them). BigQuery: not available
(Google Cloud IAM). MongoDB: not available (db user show reads them; send
grantRolesToUser with db query). --dry-run shows the statement.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or

  komando db grant prod-db app_ro --role readers --dry-run
  komando db grant prod-db app_ro --role readers --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db grant prod-db app --privileges SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE --on 'shop.*' --dry-run
  komando db grant prod-db app --privileges SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE --on 'shop.*' --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

Flags:
      --from-host string    MySQL: where the user connects from (the account host; default %)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for grant
      --on string           what the privileges are on (see above)
      --privileges string   comma-separated: SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE,DELETE,... or ALL
      --role string         make the user a member of this role

      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv

### komando db kill --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Find the PID with `komando db activity` or `komando db locks`. Without
--session only the running query stops (its transaction rolls back) and the
client stays connected. --dry-run shows the session it would stop. SQL
Server can only end a session (KILL), so there it needs --session. On Oracle
the PID is the SID that db activity shows. On ClickHouse it is the number db
activity shows for the query (made from its query_id); ClickHouse stops
queries, not connections, so there is no --session. On Snowflake, too, the
PID is the number db activity shows for the query; --session ends its
session (SYSTEM$ABORT_SESSION). On BigQuery it is the number db activity
shows for a job, which db kill cancels (jobs.cancel); there is no --session.
On MongoDB the PID is the opid that db activity shows; db kill stops that
operation (killOp) and the client stays connected, so there is no --session.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando db kill CONN PID [flags]

Examples:
  komando db kill prod-db 4821 --dry-run
  komando db kill prod-db 4821
  komando db kill prod-db 4821 --session --dry-run
  komando db kill prod-db 4821 --session --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for kill
      --session[=true|false]   end the whole connection, not just its query

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit for each query (default 30s, or the conn's statement_timeout option)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando db query --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Runs SQL on a database and prints the rows. Without --write it only reads:
komando runs it in a read-only transaction, and stops it after 30s.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the query deletes data
(DROP, DELETE without WHERE, KILL, ...): dangerous, it cannot be undone: a
person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as
well.

Usage:
  komando db query CONN [SQL] [flags]

Examples:
  komando db query prod-db "select id, email from users order by id desc limit 10"
  komando db query mongo-db '{"find": "users", "filter": {"plan": "pro"}, "limit": 10}'   # MongoDB
  komando db query prod-db "select * from users where email = $1" --arg bob@example.com
  komando db query prod-db --write --dry-run "update users set plan = 'pro' where id = 42"
  komando db query prod-db --file migration.sql --write --dry-run
  komando db query prod-db -o csv "select * from orders" > orders.csv
  komando db query bq "select count(*) from shop.orders" --max-bytes 50GB   # BigQuery

Flags:
      --arg stringArray      value for a placeholder ($1 in postgres, ? in mysql/sqlite, @p1 in sqlserver, :1 in oracle, {p1:String} in clickhouse, ? in snowflake and bigquery); repeat in order
  -f, --file string          read SQL from a file ('-' for stdin)
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for query
  -n, --limit int            the most rows to return per statement (0 = no limit; --max-output caps the size too) (default 500)
      --max-bytes bytes      BigQuery: the most a query may read, which BigQuery bills by, like 50GB (default 10GB; 0 = no cap)
      --write[=true|false]   allow changes (runs in a normal transaction; combine with --dry-run to roll back)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit for each query (default 30s, or the conn's statement_timeout option)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

More about db query:
A run stops after 30s unless --timeout (or the statement_timeout option in
the database URL) allows more. Placeholders take their values from
--arg, in order. -o csv and -o tsv print every row (up to --limit, if
given) for spreadsheets and scripts.
SQL that starts with a -- comment: pass it after -- or with -f -.

SQL Server has no read-only transaction: without --write komando rolls the
SQL back, and a statement it does not know as a read (a bare procedure
name, EXEC) needs --write. Its placeholders are @p1, @p2, ...

Oracle: placeholders are :1, :2, ... A PL/SQL block (BEGIN ... END;) runs
to the end of the text or to a line with only /, and needs --write and
--allow-dangerous. DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, GRANT) commits on its own in
Oracle, so it needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.

ClickHouse has no transactions: without --write every request carries the
server's own readonly=1, and a statement that is not a read (INSERT, ALTER,
CREATE, ...) needs --write, goes on its own, and a dry run only reports it.
Placeholders are {p1:String}, {p2:UInt64}, ... (named p1, p2, with a type).

Snowflake has no read-only mode komando can switch on, and each statement
is a session of its own: without --write komando sends only what it rates
as a read, and a statement that is not a read needs --write, goes on its
own, and a dry run only reports it. Log in with a role that may only
read. Placeholders are ?.

BigQuery: each statement first goes as a dry run, which runs nothing and
says what BigQuery sees and how many bytes it would read (which is what
BigQuery bills). Without --write only a SELECT runs. A query that would
read more than --max-bytes (default 10GB) does not run, and the job
carries that cap too. A write needs --write, goes on its own, and
--write --dry-run shows BigQuery's dry run. Placeholders are ?; the values
go as STRING, so write CAST(? AS INT64) for a number.

On MongoDB the text is a command document in JSON, its first key
naming it ({"find": ...}, {"aggregate": ...}, {"update": ...}). komando rates
it as it rates SQL: what it does not know as a read needs --write. "$db"
picks another database than the URL's.
--- stderr
### komando db restore --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Runs the SQL in FILE (from `db dump`, pg_dump, mysqldump or any plain SQL
file; .gz is read compressed). komando runs the SQL itself, through the
conn's --via path, never with psql or mysql. A PostgreSQL archive (`db dump
--format custom`) is recognized by its content and loaded with pg_restore on
a server: the one named with --run-on HOST, else the database's --via
server; the archive is streamed to it over SSH.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

In a terminal komando first offers to save a copy of the database as it is
now (db dump), so you can go back. Scripts and AI agents get no question:
run `komando db dump CONN` yourself first.

A restore can overwrite existing data, so it needs --allow-dangerous, plus
--yes on a protected database. The whole file is checked first: client
commands that could run programs (\! or system) and SQL komando cannot
follow (a file ending inside a quote, a change to how quotes are read) are
refused, and SQL that runs programs, touches server files or changes
privileges is named in the approval.

PostgreSQL restores run in one transaction: on any error nothing changes.
MySQL runs the statements in order and stops at the first error.

Usage:
  komando db restore CONN --from FILE [flags]

Examples:
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod-2026-11-02.sql.gz --dry-run   # checks the file, changes nothing
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod-2026-11-02.sql.gz --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod.dump --run-on db1 --dry-run
  komando db restore staging-db --from prod.dump --run-on db1 --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

Flags:
      --from string         SQL file on this computer
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for restore
      --run-on string       run pg_restore for a PostgreSQL archive on this server (default: the database's --via server)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando db revoke --help
exit 0
--- stdout
OBJECT for PostgreSQL: database:NAME, schema:NAME, table:[SCHEMA.]TABLE or
all-tables:SCHEMA; --role ROLE takes the user out of ROLE. For MySQL: DB.*,
DB.TABLE or *.* (with --from-host for the account host). For ClickHouse:
DB.*, DB.TABLE or *.*, or database:DB, table:DB.TABLE. Snowflake: not
available (db user show reads them). BigQuery: not available (Google Cloud
IAM). MongoDB: not available (db user show reads them; send grantRolesToUser
with db query). --dry-run shows the statement.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando db revoke CONN USER [flags]

Examples:
  komando db revoke prod-db app_ro --privileges SELECT --on all-tables:public --dry-run   # shows the statement
  komando db revoke prod-db app_ro --privileges SELECT --on all-tables:public --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db revoke prod-db app_ro --role readers --dry-run
  komando db revoke prod-db app_ro --role readers --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando db revoke prod-db app --privileges SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE --on 'shop.*' --dry-run
  komando db revoke prod-db app --privileges SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE --on 'shop.*' --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

Flags:
      --from-host string    MySQL: where the user connects from (the account host; default %)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for revoke
      --on string           what the privileges are on (see above)
      --privileges string   comma-separated: SELECT,INSERT,UPDATE,DELETE,... or ALL
      --role string         take the user out of this role

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit for each query (default 30s, or the conn's statement_timeout option)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando db shell --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Opens komando's own SQL shell on CONN (PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL
Server, Oracle, ClickHouse, Snowflake, BigQuery or SQLite), through its
--via path when it has one. Nothing else needs to be installed.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Each statement ends with ; (an Oracle PL/SQL block with a line holding
only /) and runs with the checks of db query: read-only
unless the shell was started with --write, destructive statements only with
--allow-dangerous, and every statement is audited. A statement runs in its
own transaction. A protected conn asks first.

Inside: \q quits, \? lists the commands, \d [TABLE] shows tables or one
table, \l databases, \dn schemas, \du roles, \x switches expanded rows,
\timing shows how long each statement took, \i FILE runs a file, and a
statement ending in \G is shown expanded. Up and down arrows recall lines.

Usage:
  komando db shell CONN [flags]

Examples:
  komando db shell prod-db
  komando db shell staging-db --write
  komando db shell staging-db --write --dry-run

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for shell
      --write[=true|false]   allow changes in this session

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit for each query (default 30s, or the conn's statement_timeout option)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
