### komando db user --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Passwords come from a secret reference (--password-ref secret:NAME,
vault:..., aws-sm:...), so they are never typed on a command line or shown.
PostgreSQL gets a SCRAM-SHA-256 verifier komando computes, so the password
itself never reaches the server or its logs. Adding a user or changing a
password is a change (a production database asks first); removing one needs
--allow-dangerous.

Usage:
  komando db user [flags]
  komando db user [command]

Examples:
  komando db user list prod-db
  komando db user show prod-db app
  komando db user add prod-db app --password-ref secret:app-pass --dry-run
  komando db user add prod-db app --password-ref secret:app-pass --allow-dangerous

Available Commands:
  add         Create a user with a password from a secret reference
  list        List the users and roles of a database
  passwd      Set a user's password from a secret reference (rotation)
  rm          Remove a database user
  show        What a user may do: privileges on tables and databases, and its roles

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for user

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit for each query (default 30s, or the conn's statement_timeout option)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando db user [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

### komando docker --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Docker on a server over SSH. Reads need nothing; start, stop, restart, pull,
compose up and a docker run through `docker raw` change things (protected
servers need --yes); rm, prune, compose down -v and other deletes need
--allow-dangerous. The same rules apply to `docker raw`, `docker compose`
and `cluster run` on a Swarm manager.

Usage:
  komando docker [flags]
  komando docker [command]

Aliases:
  docker, container, ctr, containers

Examples:
  komando docker ps web1 --all
  komando docker logs web1 api --since 10m
  komando docker restart web1 api
  komando docker compose web1 --dir /srv/shop -- up -d
  komando docker prune web1 --dry-run               # what would be freed

Available Commands:
  compose     Run docker compose for a project folder
  exec        Run a command in a container (its words are passed as given, no shell)
  images      Images on the server
  inspect     Show a container, image or other object in full (docker inspect)
  logs        Read a container's logs
  prune       Free disk space: stopped containers, unused images, build cache
  ps          Running containers (--all for stopped ones too)
  pull        Pull images from their registry (docker pull)
  raw         Run any docker subcommand (the same safety rules apply)
  restart     Restart containers (docker restart)
  rm          Remove containers
  start       Start stopped containers (docker start)
  stats       CPU, memory, network and disk use of running containers
  stop        Stop running containers (docker stop)

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for docker
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]   run docker with sudo

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando docker [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

### komando docker exec --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Runs COMMAND in the container with its arguments exactly as written (like
`docker exec`): no shell is added, so the image needs no sh. For pipes or
&& write the shell yourself: -- sh -c 'a | b'. The destructive-command
policy checks the command; --read-only declares that it only looks: only
commands komando knows only read run, and a protected server then needs
no --yes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando docker exec TARGET CONTAINER -- COMMAND... [flags]

Examples:
  komando docker exec app1 api -- php artisan migrate:status
  komando docker exec app1 api --read-only -- sh -c 'ls /data | wc -l'

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for exec
      --read-only[=true|false]   declare that the command only looks (protected servers: no --yes for commands komando knows read)
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        run docker with sudo

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

exit 0

The last lines of a container's log (-n, default 200), or new lines as they
come with -f. --since and --until take a time back from now (10m, 2h, 7d)
or a date (2026-01-02T10:00:00). --sudo runs docker with sudo.

Examples:

  komando docker logs web1 api --follow

      --grep string               only lines matching this extended regex (case-insensitive)
  -h, --help[=true|false]         help for logs
  -n, --limit int                 the most lines to show (the last ones) (default 200)
      --since string              start time: back from now (30m, 2h, 7d), today, yesterday or '2026-01-02 10:00'
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]         read via sudo (the whole journal, protected files)
      --timestamps[=true|false]   show when each container log line was written (containers)
      --until string              end time, in the same forms as --since

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also

      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando docker prune --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Runs docker system prune on the server. It removes stopped containers,
dangling images (--all: every image no container uses), unused networks
and build cache; with --volumes also unused anonymous volumes and the data
in them.
--older-than 30d keeps everything made in the last 30 days. Docker has no
age filter for volumes, so with --volumes komando reads each unused
anonymous volume's creation time and removes only the older ones
(docker volume rm NAME), after the prune.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--dry-run changes nothing: it lists what would go, with sizes and a total,
read from docker on the server. The real run deletes and needs
--allow-dangerous; a protected server needs --yes too.

Usage:
  komando docker prune TARGET [flags]

Examples:
  komando docker prune web1 --dry-run
  komando docker prune web1 --older-than 30d --all --dry-run
  komando docker prune web1 --older-than 30d --dry-run
  komando docker prune web1 --older-than 30d --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando docker prune web1 --volumes --older-than 30d --dry-run

Flags:
  -a, --all[=true|false]       every image no container uses, not only dangling ones
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for prune
      --older-than duration    only what is older than this (like 30d, 12h)
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]      run docker with sudo
      --volumes[=true|false]   also unused anonymous volumes (their data is lost)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

--- stderr
### komando download --help
exit 0
--- stdout
PATH is the path on the servers, or the key in the storage conn. --to is
where it lands: a file name, or a folder (existing, or ending in /); a
folder per server when several are picked. A file that is already here is
replaced only with --overwrite: without it, one file stops with FILE_EXISTS,
and a folder keeps them (kept) and copies the rest. --sudo reads one file
as root (up to 512 MiB).

--to - streams one file to stdout, from a server or storage: stdout has the
file's bytes and nothing else, whatever -o says, and komando's own answer
(the result with bytes and sha256, or the error) goes to stderr.

--continue goes on with a download of one file that was cut off: the part
already here is kept when it matches the source (sha256), the rest is
fetched, and the whole file is checked. A file here that is longer, or
differs, stops with RESUME_CONFLICT and is not touched.

Folders (-r), like cp and rsync:
  PATH/  (trailing slash)  the contents of PATH go into --to
  PATH   into a new --to    --to becomes the copy of PATH
  PATH   into a folder --to of the same name (/var/log/app -> ./app): it
         is updated in place, so downloading again never nests app/app
  PATH   into another existing folder --to: the copy is --to/NAME
Without --to it lands in the current folder under its own name. Symbolic
links are not copied (they are listed as skipped).

Usage:
  komando download TARGET PATH [flags]

Examples:
  komando download web1 /var/log/nginx/error.log --to ./logs/
  komando download @web /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --to ./configs/
  komando download backups 2026/db.sql.gz
  komando download backups reports/ -r --to ./reports
  komando download web1 /var/backups/db.sql.gz --continue
  komando download web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --to - > nginx.conf

Flags:
      --continue[=true|false]    go on with a copy that was cut off: keep the part already at the destination when it matches the source, send the rest, then check the whole file (sha256)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for download
      --overwrite[=true|false]   replace files that already exist on this computer
      --progress[=true|false]    with -o json, write progress to the error output (stderr), one JSON object per line
  -r, --recursive[=true|false]   download a folder (servers) or every object under a prefix (storage)
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        read the file as root (single files)
      --to string                where to save it, or - to stream it to stdout (default: the current folder)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

  KOMANDO_HOME        where komando keeps its data (default ~/.komando)

What komando's exit codes mean.

  7 timeout     8 precondition or conflict

### komando export --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Saves your list to a file (komando-export/1, always JSON) that
`komando import komando FILE` reads on another computer. Passwords and key
files are never in it (only in a sealed file); it lists the secrets and keys
to bring along. With a
TARGET (@prod, kind:host, web1,web2) only those servers, conns and VPNs are
saved; without one also your recipes, deny rules and settings. Without --to
it prints the same JSON.

Safety: it only reads; with --sealed: only a person at a terminal can run
it; with --for-phone: only a person at a terminal can run it; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--sealed writes the same list with the passwords it uses into one sealed
file, for moving to another computer: komando asks for a passphrase twice
(15 or more characters), hidden, and the file opens only with it.
--for-phone seals the file to the iPhone app's key instead: komando asks
for the key file the phone shared and the key check the phone shows. Both
print a check phrase of six words; the phone shows the same words for the
file it got. --with-keys adds the private keys the servers use.

Only a person at a terminal can make a sealed file: an AI agent gets
NEEDS_PERSON, and a dry run says what would be sealed.

Usage:
  komando export [TARGET] [flags]

Examples:
  komando export --to komando-backup.json
  komando export @prod --to prod.json
  komando export kind:host --to servers.json
  komando import komando komando-backup.json      # on the other computer
  komando export --sealed --to move.kmdseal       # with passwords; asks a passphrase
  komando export --for-phone --to phone.kmdseal   # for the iPhone app; asks for its key

Flags:
      --for-phone[=true|false]   seal the file to the iPhone app's key, with the passwords in it (a person at a terminal; needs --to)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for export
      --overwrite[=true|false]   replace the file if it exists
      --sealed[=true|false]      seal the file with a passphrase, with the passwords in it (a person at a terminal; needs --to)
      --to string                write to this file (0600) instead of printing
      --with-keys[=true|false]   with --sealed or --for-phone: also the private keys the servers use

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando facts --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Run this first on a server you do not know yet: it tells an agent which
package manager, init system and tools exist, so later commands fit the
server.

It also reports what needs attention: whether the OS still gets security
updates (Ubuntu ESM, Debian LTS, end of life), pending and security updates
(from the server's package index, which it does not refresh), a needed
reboot, passwordless sudo, Docker and the Swarm role, PM2 apps, listening
ports and services added by hand under /etc/systemd/system.

On Windows servers it reports the Windows version and its support dates,
pending updates from the Windows Update cache, a pending reboot, stopped
automatic services and listening ports.

--only load,mem,disks runs just those probes (load and CPUs; memory and
swap; every file system), in about a second, for an app that polls; the
other keys are left out. --only system gives the OS name and version and
the time the server has been up. On Windows the full probe runs and only
those keys are kept.

It only reads, and it uses sudo only when sudo works without a password.
A value komando cannot read is null ("unknown"), never 0 or false; read
data.results[].data.warnings first.

Usage:
  komando facts TARGET [flags]

Aliases:
  facts, info

Examples:
  komando facts web1
  komando facts @prod -o json
  komando facts web1 --only load,mem,disks -o json
  komando facts web1 --only system

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for facts
      --only strings        run only these sections, comma-separated: disks, load, mem, system (fast, for polling; the other keys are left out)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando fs --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Reads and changes files on servers over SFTP and returns structured results.
Use --sudo for files that root owns: a read runs `sudo cat`, a write goes to
a temporary file first and then into place with `sudo install`.

For an agent, `fs replace` is the way to edit a config file: it fails unless
the old text matches exactly once (or --all), and --backup keeps a .bak
copy.

Usage:
  komando fs [flags]
  komando fs [command]

Aliases:
  fs, files

Examples:
  komando fs list web1 /etc/nginx
  komando fs cat web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 512' --new 'worker_connections 1024' --backup --dry-run
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 512' --new 'worker_connections 1024' --backup
  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf     # undo the edit

Available Commands:
  cat         Read a file on one server
  chmod       Change the mode of paths on servers
  list        List a folder on one server (default: the login user's home)
  mkdir       Create folders on servers, with any missing parents
  mv          Move or rename a path on servers
  replace     Edit a file on servers by replacing exact text
  restore     Undo a file edit by putting back its backup copy
  rm          Remove files on servers
  stat        Look up a path on one server (exists:false, not an error, when missing)
  write       Write a file on one server, all or nothing

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for fs

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando fs [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

Moves SRC to DST. When DST is an existing folder, SRC moves into it (like

### komando fs replace --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Replaces --old with --new in PATH. On a group (@web) every server gets the
same edit; each server's result says what changed there, and a server where
--old is not found fails on its own (NO_MATCH) while the others are changed.
Run it with --dry-run first to see each server's diff.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando fs replace TARGET PATH --old TEXT --new TEXT [flags]

Examples:
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 768;' --new 'worker_connections 4096;' --sudo --backup
  komando fs replace @web /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --old 'worker_connections 768;' --new 'worker_connections 4096;' --sudo --backup --dry-run
  komando fs replace web1 /etc/ssh/sshd_config --regex --old '(?m)^#?PasswordAuthentication .*$' --new 'PasswordAuthentication no' --sudo

Flags:
      --all[=true|false]         replace every occurrence
      --backup[=true|false]      keep the previous version as PATH.bak (PATH.bak.<UTC time> when that exists; a backup is never overwritten)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for replace
      --mode string              file mode, like 0640 (default: keep existing or 0644)
      --new string               the text to put in its place ($1 for a group with --regex)
      --no-follow[=true|false]   refuse to write through a symbolic link (by default the file it points to is written and the link stays)
      --old string               the text to find (a regular expression with --regex)
      --owner string             owner[:group] (needs --sudo)
  -p, --parents[=true|false]     create missing parent folders
      --regex[=true|false]       treat --old as a Go regular expression
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        write with sudo (for files root owns)
      --validate string          check the new file before it goes into place; %s is its path (like 'visudo -cf %s', 'nginx -t -c %s')

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)

### komando fs restore --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Puts back the newest backup of PATH that fs write or fs replace --backup
made (PATH.bak, or PATH.bak.<UTC time> when there are several). The file as
it is now is kept as a new backup first, so you can undo the restore too.
On a group (@web) each server puts back its own newest backup. Add --dry-run
to see the change without making it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando fs restore TARGET PATH [flags]

Examples:
  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --sudo --dry-run
  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --sudo
  komando fs restore @web /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --sudo --dry-run
  komando fs restore web1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --copy /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.bak --sudo

Flags:
      --copy string         the backup copy to put back, a path on the server (default: the newest PATH.bak)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for restore
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]   read and write with sudo (for files root owns)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando fs rm --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Removes files like rm -f: a path that does not exist is reported ("not
found") and the command still succeeds. A folder needs --recursive, which
also needs --allow-dangerous. Paths are taken literally: '*.log' is not a
pattern (use komando host ssh exec for that).

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando fs rm TARGET PATH... [flags]

Aliases:
  rm, remove, delete, del

Examples:
  komando fs rm web1 /tmp/upload.tar.gz
  komando fs rm web1 /tmp/upload.tar.gz --dry-run
  komando fs rm web1 /srv/app/releases/old --recursive --dry-run
  komando fs rm web1 /srv/app/releases/old --recursive --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for rm
  -r, --recursive[=true|false]   remove folders and everything in them
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        run with sudo

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or

### komando guide install --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Teaches Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI to use komando safely.
Then restart the agent. In Codex, also approve the guard once in /hooks.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

It adds the komando skill (komando/SKILL.md) to the folders AI agents read
skills from: ~/.claude/skills (Claude Code) and ~/.agents/skills (Codex,
Cursor, Gemini CLI and others). The agent then uses komando by itself
whenever a task touches a server, database, cache or storage.

It also adds a guard: before the agent reads a file or runs a shell command
on this computer, komando checks it and stops the ones that would read
secrets (~/.komando, private keys, .env files, credential stores, all
environment variables at once) or use ssh around komando. It goes into
Claude Code (.claude/settings.json), and into Cursor (.cursor/hooks.json),
Gemini CLI (.gemini/settings.json, v0.26+) and Codex (.codex/hooks.json;
approve it once in /hooks) where their folders exist. Skip it with
--no-guard.

Safe to run again, for example after an update: a changed file is kept as
.bak. `komando guide uninstall` takes the skill and the guard out again.

Usage:
  komando guide install [flags]

Examples:
  komando guide install             # for every project on this computer
  komando guide install --project   # only for the folder you are in
  komando guide install --dry-run   # show where it would go

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]       help for install
      --no-guard[=true|false]   do not add the guard that keeps AI agents away from secret files on this computer
      --project[=true|false]    install into the current folder instead of your home folder

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando guide uninstall --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Removes what `komando guide install` added: komando/SKILL.md in
~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills, and komando's guard entries in
.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .gemini/settings.json and
.codex/hooks.json. Everything else in those files stays; a changed file is
kept as .bak. Taking the guard away from an AI agent lets it read secret
files on this computer again, so an agent needs a person's yes (--yes).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it removes komando's
guard from an AI agent's settings: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes
(--yes).

Usage:
  komando guide uninstall [flags]

Examples:
  komando guide uninstall             # from your home folder
  komando guide uninstall --project   # from the folder you are in
  komando guide uninstall --dry-run   # show what it would remove

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for uninstall
      --project[=true|false]   remove from the current folder instead of your home folder

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)

### komando host ca --help
exit 0
--- stdout
A host CA vouches for the host keys of the servers its patterns match, as an
@cert-authority line in known_hosts does. A server that shows a host
certificate from a trusted CA, for the name komando dials, is trusted
without a pin. Adding a CA trusts every server it ever signs, so only a
person at a terminal can add one. Removing one, and putting a key on the
never-trust list, anyone may do.

Usage:
  komando host ca [flags]
  komando host ca [command]

Examples:
  komando host ca add corp --key ~/corp-ca.pub --hosts '*.corp.example' --dry-run
  komando host ca list
  komando host ca rm corp
  komando host ca revoke --key old-ca.pub

Available Commands:
  add         Trust a CA for the servers its patterns match (person only)
  list        List the trusted server CAs
  revoke      Never trust a host key or a CA key again
  rm          Stop trusting a server CA

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for ca

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando host ca [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando host ca add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Trusts the CA in --key (a .pub file) for the host names in --hosts, or reads
the @cert-authority lines of a known_hosts file (--from); its @revoked lines
go on the never-trust list. A pattern names at least the domain
(*.corp.example, web*.corp.example, 10.1.2.*): '*' and '*.com' are refused.
--dry-run shows the patterns as they are kept and the servers they match
now. Only a person at a terminal can add a CA: it trusts every server it
ever signs.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Usage:
  komando host ca add NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando host ca add corp --key ~/corp-ca.pub --hosts '*.corp.example' --dry-run
  komando host ca add corp --from ~/.ssh/known_hosts

Flags:
      --from string         a known_hosts file: read its @cert-authority and @revoked lines
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for add
      --hosts strings       server name patterns the CA may vouch for (*.corp.example,10.1.2.*)
      --key string          the CA's public key file (.pub)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando host ssh --help
exit 0
--- stdout
SSH servers: save them, run commands on them, tunnel through them

Usage:
  komando host ssh [flags]
  komando host ssh [command]

Examples:
  komando host ssh add web1 deploy@10.0.0.5 --dry-run
  komando host ssh add web1 deploy@10.0.0.5
  komando host ssh test web1
  komando host ssh exec web1 -- uptime
  komando host ssh tunnel start db1 -L 15432:localhost:5432

Available Commands:
  add         Save an SSH server under a short name
  edit        Change saved SSH servers (only the flags you pass change)
  exec        Run a command on saved servers, in parallel
  list        List the saved SSH servers
  remove      Forget saved SSH servers (the servers are not touched)
  rename      Rename a saved ssh server and every reference to it
  shell       Open a login shell on one server (a person at a terminal) (person only)
  show        Show a saved ssh server's settings (credentials as names)
  test        Check that saved SSH servers answer and let you in
  trust       Pin the SSH host keys of servers (--reset after a rebuild)
  tunnel      Background tunnels through a server: start, list, stop

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for ssh

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando host ssh [command] --help" for more information about a command.

### komando host ssh add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Save an SSH server under a short name.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when --proxy-command matches
a destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name
to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; with
--proxy-command, when an AI agent runs it (the proxy command runs on this
computer): it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

Usage:
  komando host ssh add NAME [ADDRESS] [flags]

Examples:
  komando host ssh add web1 deploy@10.0.0.11 --group web --tag prod
  komando host ssh add web1 deploy@10.0.0.11 --dry-run
  komando host ssh add db1 --address db.internal --user root --via web1 --protected

Flags:
      --address string              the host name or IP address, instead of the second word
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored as a password credential
      --credential string           what it logs in with
  -e, --env stringArray             env KEY=VALUE exported before every command (default [])
      --group strings               put it in these groups
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --identity string             the path of a private key file
      --key string                  the name of a key in komando's key list
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --login string                how komando logs in: ask at every connect, a stored password, a key, or the ssh-agent
      --notes string                free-form notes, shown to people and agents
      --os string                   the server's OS: windows runs commands in PowerShell
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace an entry that has the same name
      --port int                    the port
      --protected[=true|false]      changes need a person's yes
      --proxy-command string        a program on this computer that makes the connection
      --ssm[=true|false]            reach it through AWS Systems Manager; the address is the instance ID
      --sudo-credential string      the password sudo asks for (today's --sudo-ref)
      --tag strings                 tags, like prod
      --user string                 the user to log in as
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

      --proxy-command string         a program on this computer that makes the connection
      --rm-group strings             take it out of these groups
      --rm-tag strings               remove these tags
      --sudo-credential string       the password sudo asks for (today's --sudo-ref)
      --unset strings                clear these settings: user, key, identity, credential, sudo-credential, via, proxy-command, notes, port, protected, forward-agent, os, transport
      --user string                  the user to log in as
      --via string                   reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

### komando host ssh exec --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Run a command on saved servers, in parallel.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando host ssh exec TARGET [-- COMMAND...] [flags]

Examples:
  komando host ssh exec web1 -- uptime
  komando host ssh exec @web -P 20 -- 'df -h / | tail -1'
  komando host ssh exec db1 --read-only -- df -h
  komando host ssh exec @web --script ./deploy.sh --arg v1.2.3 --sudo

Flags:
      --arg stringArray          an argument for the script, $1 and on
      --attach strings           read the rest of these sessions on one server, and their exit codes
  -c, --cmd string               the command as one string, instead of the words after --
  -C, --dir string               the working folder on the server
  -e, --env stringArray          export KEY=VALUE before the command
      --fail-fast[=true|false]   start no more servers after the first failure
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for exec
      --interpreter string       the interpreter on the server (default: from the #! line, else sh)
      --log-max bytes            bytes of output the server keeps for the run; more is dropped (default 1GiB)
      --offset int               start at this byte of the log (next_from of the last read)
      --pty[=true|false]         ask for a pseudo-terminal (some tools need one)
      --read-only[=true|false]   the command only reads (the policy checks it either way)
      --remove[=true|false]      remove a finished session's log from the server
      --script string            run this script from this computer ('-' is komando's stdin); nothing is left on the server
      --signal string            the signal --stop sends (default "TERM")
      --stdin-file string        send this file as stdin ('-' is komando's stdin)
      --stop[=true|false]        stop the session's command
      --stream[=true|false]      print the output as NDJSON events while it runs
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        run with sudo (it never prompts; it uses the server's sudo credential)
      --sudo-user string         run as this user with sudo -u
      --wait duration            wait this long for the run to end; it goes on after (exit 7); 0 returns at once (default 1m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando host ssh-command --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Prints the ssh command that reaches the server with the same address, user,
key, known_hosts file and --via path komando uses. A server behind --via
servers gets a ProxyCommand per hop (ssh -W), so every hop uses its own key.
A SOCKS VPN becomes nc -X 5; VPNs that run inside komando cannot be used by
OpenSSH: use `komando host ssh shell SERVER` for those. A key made with
komando key gen is never written to a file: it goes to your running
ssh-agent (SSH_AUTH_SOCK) for one hour, and the line picks it by its public
key.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Usage:
  komando host ssh-command NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando host ssh-command web1
  $(komando host ssh-command web1 -o text)      # open a shell with OpenSSH

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for ssh-command

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

  -e, --env stringArray             env KEY=VALUE exported before every command (default [])
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for edit
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --login string                how komando logs in: ask at every connect, a stored password, a key, or the ssh-agent
      --notes string                free-form notes, shown to people and agents
      --port int                    the port
      --protected[=true|false]      changes need a person's yes
      --rm-group strings            take it out of these groups
      --rm-tag strings              remove these tags
      --unset strings               clear these settings: user, credential, via, notes, port, protected
      --user string                 the user to log in as
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando import --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Adds servers, conns, VPNs and recipes from files you already have.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; SOURCE kubeconfig, when an AI
agent imports a context whose login runs a program or sends a file of this
computer: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); SOURCE komando,
when the file is sealed (export --sealed): a person types its passphrase:
only a person at a terminal can run it; when an imported proxy command
matches a destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types
the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; when
an AI agent imports a server with a proxy command: it weakens a safety
check: a person's yes (--yes).

Sources:
  ssh-config  servers from your OpenSSH config (default ~/.ssh/config)
  pgpass      PostgreSQL databases and their passwords (default ~/.pgpass)
  mycnf       MySQL/MariaDB databases from [client] sections (default ~/.my.cnf)
  env         database, cache and storage URLs (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, ...) (default .env)
  kubeconfig  Kubernetes clusters, one conn per context (default ~/.kube/config)
  docker      container registries you are logged in to (default ~/.docker/config.json)
  filezilla   SFTP sites from FileZilla's Site Manager (default ~/.config/filezilla/sitemanager.xml)
  rclone      SFTP remotes from rclone (default ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf)
  putty       SSH sessions from PuTTY (a .reg file: `reg export HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions putty.reg`)
  mobaxterm   SSH sessions from MobaXterm (a .mxtsessions file: right-click User sessions, Export all sessions to file)
  securecrt   SSH2 sessions from SecureCRT (File > Export Settings gives an .xml file; or its Sessions folder)
  aws         an S3 storage conn per bucket of each AWS profile (uses the profile; no key is copied) (default ~/.aws/config)
  aws-ec2     a server per running EC2 instance of each AWS profile, in its region (read only, with the profile's login) (default ~/.aws/config)
  dbeaver     databases from DBeaver (passwords set afterwards) (default ~/Library/DBeaverData/workspace6/General/.dbeaver/data-sources.json)
  komando     a file made by `komando export` (moving to another computer)
  csv         servers from a spreadsheet (CSV, first row names the columns: name, address (or ip), user, port, key, identity, password-ref, sudo-ref, via, groups (or role), tags, protected, notes)

Passwords go to the vault (as <name>-pass; a kubeconfig as
<name>-kubeconfig) and are referenced from the conn; they are never
printed. Existing names are skipped unless
--overwrite (replacing a protected one also needs --yes). Proxy commands
from an ssh config run on this computer, so an AI agent needs a person's yes
for them. Try --dry-run first to see what would be added.

Usage:
  komando import SOURCE [FILE] [flags]

Examples:
  komando import ssh-config --dry-run
  komando import pgpass
  komando import env ./app/.env --group shop
  komando import komando backup.json

Flags:
  -g, --group strings            add everything imported to these groups
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for import
      --overwrite[=true|false]   replace servers, conns and recipes with the same name

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando job --help
exit 0
--- stdout
A long command should not hold up an agent's tool call. `job start` starts
the command in the background on each server and returns the job IDs at
once; it keeps running when the connection drops. Check on it with `job
status` or `job logs --offset N` (pass back next_offset), or wait with `job
wait --timeout`.

Usage:
  komando job [flags]
  komando job [command]

Aliases:
  job, jobs

Examples:
  komando job start @web -- ./deploy.sh
  komando job list
  komando job wait j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --timeout 30m
  komando job logs j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --limit 50

Available Commands:
  kill        Stop a job: send a signal to its process group (default TERM)
  list        List the jobs komando started (--refresh asks the servers)
  logs        Read a job's output, piece by piece or its last lines
  rm          Forget jobs and delete their logs on the server
  start       Start a background job on each server TARGET picks
  status      Show a job's state, exit code, run time and last lines
  wait        Wait until the jobs end

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for job

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando job [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

### komando job start --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Starts COMMAND in the background on each server TARGET picks and returns
the job IDs at once; the job keeps running when the connection drops.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the command matches a
destructive rule: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to
go on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

--script FILE runs a script from this computer as the job, like
`exec --script`: it goes to the interpreter (from its #! line, else sh;
--interpreter to choose) and its copy on the server is removed as soon as
the job has opened it. --arg values become $1, $2 ... .

--stdin-file FILE is the command's input ('-' for komando's own stdin), as
in exec. --sudo-user USER runs it as USER with sudo -u. --timeout stops the
job after that long (as job kill does; job status then says it timed out);
without it a job has no time limit.

Usage:
  komando job start TARGET -- COMMAND... [flags]

Examples:
  komando job start db1 -- 'pg_dump app | gzip > /backup/app.sql.gz'
  komando job start @web --sudo -- 'apt-get update && apt-get -y upgrade'
  komando job start @web --script ./deploy.sh --arg v1.2.3 --sudo
  komando job start db1 --sudo-user postgres --stdin-file ./migrate.sql --timeout 2h -- 'psql app'

Flags:
      --arg stringArray          with --script: an argument for the script, $1 ... (repeatable)
  -c, --cmd string               the command as one string (instead of words after --)
  -C, --dir string               working folder on the server
  -e, --env stringArray          export KEY=VALUE before the command (repeatable)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for start
      --interpreter string       with --script: the interpreter on the server (default: from the #! line, else sh)
      --read-only[=true|false]   declare that the command only looks (protected servers: no --yes for commands komando knows read)
      --script string            run this script from this computer as the job ('-' = komando's stdin)
      --stdin-file string        send this file on this computer as the command's input ('-' = komando's stdin)
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        run with sudo (uses the server's --sudo-ref password if set)
      --sudo-user string         run as this user with sudo -u
      --timeout duration         stop the job after this long, like 2h (default: no limit)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando job wait --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Waits until the job ends, checking every --interval. --timeout (default 10m)
is how long to wait; the job keeps running after it (exit 7, WAIT_TIMEOUT).

A dropped connection does not stop the wait: komando connects again and
keeps waiting. Give several job IDs (the ones `job start` printed for a
group of servers) to wait for all of them at once.

Usage:
  komando job wait JOB... [flags]

Examples:
  komando job wait j1103-101500-ab12cd34 --timeout 30m
  komando job wait j1103-101500-ab12cd34 j1103-101500-ef56ab78

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for wait
      --interval duration   how often to check (default 3s)
      --tail int            also show the last N lines of output (default 30)
      --timeout duration    how long to wait (the job keeps running after) (default 10m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando key --help
exit 0
--- stdout
SSH keys: make, add, put on servers, take off

Usage:
  komando key [flags]
  komando key [command]

Aliases:
  key, keys

Examples:
  komando key gen deploy
  komando key deploy deploy @web --dry-run
  komando key deploy deploy @web
  komando key list

Available Commands:
  add         Add a private key file you already have (komando keeps its path)
  deploy      Install a public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (like ssh-copy-id)
  edit        Change a key's passphrase reference or certificate
  gen         Make a new SSH key pair (ed25519 by default)
  list        List keys and the servers that use them
  rename      Rename a key, and every server that uses it
  revoke      Take a public key off servers' authorized_keys
  rm          Remove a key (from komando only)
  show        Show a key's public part, or a person its private key

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for key

  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando key [command] --help" for more information about a command.

### komando key add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Adds a private key file you already have to komando's key list; the file
stays where it is. For a key with a passphrase, store the passphrase in the
vault and pass --passphrase-ref secret:NAME.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

An OpenSSH user certificate next to the key (FILE-cert.pub) is used at
login, as ssh does; --cert names one kept somewhere else.

Usage:
  komando key add NAME FILE [flags]

Examples:
  komando key add personal ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  komando key add personal ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 --dry-run
  komando key add corp ~/.ssh/id_corp --cert ~/.ssh/corp-ca/id_corp-cert.pub
  komando secret set id-pass && komando key add work ~/.ssh/id_work --passphrase-ref secret:id-pass

Flags:
      --cert string             an OpenSSH user certificate for the key (default: FILE-cert.pub next to it, if there)
  -h, --help[=true|false]       help for add
      --passphrase-ref string   passphrase reference for encrypted keys (secret:NAME | env:VAR | ...)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando key deploy --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Installs a public key on servers, like ssh-copy-id. KEY is a key in
komando's key list or a .pub file. komando logs in the way each server is
set up now (a password, for example) and appends the key to
~/.ssh/authorized_keys unless it is already there. With --set-default the
servers then log in with this key.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando key deploy NAME TARGET [flags]

Examples:
  komando key gen deploy && komando key deploy deploy @web --set-default
  komando key deploy ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub web1
  komando key deploy ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub web1 --dry-run

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]          help for deploy
      --set-default[=true|false]   servers that got the key log in with it from now on

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando key edit --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Sets where komando finds the passphrase of an encrypted key. Store the
passphrase with `komando secret set NAME` first and pass secret:NAME;
--unset passphrase-ref clears it.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

--cert FILE gives the key an OpenSSH user certificate (for a key komando
made, or one kept away from the key file); --unset cert goes back to
FILE-cert.pub next to the key.

Usage:
  komando key edit NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando secret set work-key-pass
  komando key edit work --passphrase-ref secret:work-key-pass
  komando key edit work --passphrase-ref secret:work-key-pass --dry-run
  komando key edit work --unset passphrase-ref
  komando key edit deploy --cert ~/Downloads/deploy-cert.pub

Flags:
      --cert string             an OpenSSH user certificate for the key
  -h, --help[=true|false]       help for edit
      --passphrase-ref string   where the passphrase is: secret:NAME | env:VAR | ...
      --unset strings           clear this setting: passphrase-ref, cert

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando key gen --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Makes a key pair like ssh-keygen and adds it to komando's key list. The
private key is kept in komando's sealed store, never in a file: komando
hands it to ssh-agent when another program needs it (host ssh-command). Put
the public part on servers with `komando key deploy`. RSA keys need at least
3072 bits.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando key gen NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando key gen deploy && komando key deploy deploy @web
  komando key gen legacy --type rsa -b 4096 -C ops@example.com
  komando key gen legacy --type rsa -b 4096 -C ops@example.com --dry-run

Flags:
  -b, --bits int            key size: RSA 3072-16384 (default 4096), ECDSA 256|384|521
  -C, --comment string      public key comment (default komando-NAME)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for gen
      --type string         ed25519 | rsa | ecdsa (default "ed25519")

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando key rename --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Gives a key in komando's key list a new name; the servers that use it
follow. A key komando made (key gen) lives in the sealed store, so no file
moves; a key added from elsewhere (key add) stays where it is. Public keys
already installed on servers keep their comment: they still work, since the
key itself does not change.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando key rename OLD NEW [flags]

Aliases:
  rename, mv

Examples:

  komando key rename old-ci ci --dry-run

### komando key revoke --help
exit 0
--- stdout
KEY is a key in komando's key list, a .pub file, or a public key line. Every
line with that key is removed from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of the login user,
or of --user NAME (with sudo), or of every user on the server with
--all-users (with sudo: someone who left may have put the key in another
account too; the dry run names each user whose file holds it). The file
keeps its owner and mode, and is read and written as its user. Revoking the
key komando itself logs in with needs --allow-dangerous: you would lock
yourself out. --dry-run counts the lines it would remove.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it is the key komando
logs in with: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go
on, and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected
server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando key revoke NAME TARGET [flags]

Examples:
  komando key revoke ~/keys/alice.pub @prod --dry-run
  komando key revoke "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nz...xyz alice@laptop" @prod
  komando key revoke old-deploy @web --user deploy
  komando key revoke ~/keys/alice.pub @prod --all-users --dry-run

Flags:
      --all-users[=true|false]   edit every user's authorized_keys on the server (uses sudo)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for revoke
      --user string              edit this user's authorized_keys instead of the login user's (uses sudo)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando key show --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Shows a key's type, fingerprint and public part. A person at a terminal can
add --reveal to print the private key of a key komando made (it is kept in
komando's sealed store, with no file), for example to keep a copy in a
password manager; from a program without a terminal (the Komando Mac app),
komando first asks the person in its own window. A key added with `key add`
is a file you have already: --reveal names its path. AI agents never get a
private key.

Usage:
  komando key show NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando key show deploy
  komando key show deploy --reveal > deploy.key   # a person, at a terminal

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for show

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando logs --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Read logs from journald (--unit), a file (--file) or a container
(--container).

Usage:
  komando logs TARGET [flags]

Examples:
  komando logs web1 --unit nginx --since 30m --grep 'error|crit'
  komando logs @web --file /var/log/nginx/error.log -n 50 --sudo
  komando logs app1 --container api --since 10m

Flags:
  -c, --container string          read this Docker container's log (its name or ID)
      --file string               read this log file on the server (full path)
  -f, --follow[=true|false]       keep printing new lines until Ctrl-C
      --grep string               only lines matching this extended regex (case-insensitive)
  -h, --help[=true|false]         help for logs
  -n, --limit int                 the most lines to show (the last ones) (default 200)
  -p, --priority string           journal priority and worse: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug (or 0-7)
      --since string              start time: back from now (30m, 2h, 7d), today, yesterday or '2026-01-02 10:00'
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]         read via sudo (the whole journal, protected files)
      --timestamps[=true|false]   show when each container log line was written (containers)
  -u, --unit string               systemd unit (journalctl)
      --until string              end time, in the same forms as --since

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando output --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Text for people, JSON for programs.

In a terminal komando prints text; piped, one JSON envelope on stdout:
  {"ok":true,"command":"exec","data":{...},"meta":{...}}
  {"ok":false,"command":"exec","error":{"code":"AUTH_FAILED",...}}
Force one with -o json or -o text (db query also takes csv and tsv).
Questions, the line komando runs ($ komando ...) and Next: go to stderr,
and only at a person's terminal.

Packages on servers through apt, dnf, yum, apk, zypper or pacman (komando

### komando pkg security --help
exit 0
--- stdout
This only looks: the pending security updates of each server (apt:
packages from the -security pocket; dnf/yum: updates with a security
notice; zypper: security patches; pacman: what arch-audit names), and the
server's state: running containers, failed units, pending updates,
whether a reboot is required, and services that run old code. Where the
repositories publish no security notices (apk, pacman without
arch-audit, some dnf/yum repositories), security_notices is false and
unclassified_updates lists every pending update.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

To install them: `komando pkg upgrade TARGET --security`, one server at a
time with a check before and after each.

Usage:
  komando pkg security TARGET [flags]

Examples:
  komando pkg security @swarm --refresh
  komando pkg upgrade @swarm --security --dry-run
  komando pkg upgrade @swarm --security

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for security
      --no-sudo[=true|false]   do not use sudo (like when logged in as root)
      --refresh[=true|false]   refresh the package index first (like apt-get update)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando pkg upgrade --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Without --security: upgrades every package, or the given ones (--dry-run
lists what would change).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --security, when an
update would remove a package the server needs: dangerous, it cannot be
undone: a person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a script needs
--allow-dangerous; on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as
well.

--security installs only the security updates, one server at a time. On
apt servers komando uses unattended-upgrade when it is installed (it picks
security origins only and follows the server's own settings), otherwise
apt-get --only-upgrade of the listed packages, keeping changed config
files. On dnf/yum it runs "upgrade --security", on zypper "patch
--category security". needrestart is kept from
restarting services during the run; the result lists the services that
need it.

After each server komando compares the state with the one before. When
fewer containers run or a unit has failed, it stops and leaves the other
servers as they are (--keep-going patches them anyway). It never reboots:
reboot_required says when a server needs one, use `komando reboot`.

The upgrade runs detached on the server, so a dropped connection does not
break it. It waits up to 30 minutes per server (--timeout changes it).
Where komando cannot pick the security updates (apk, pacman, dnf/yum
repositories without security notices) the server stops with
SECURITY_UNSUPPORTED: use `komando pkg upgrade` without --security there.

Usage:
  komando pkg upgrade TARGET [PACKAGE...] [flags]

Examples:
  komando pkg upgrade web1 --dry-run   # see what would change first
  komando pkg upgrade web1 openssl
  komando pkg upgrade @web --security --dry-run
  komando pkg upgrade @web --security

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]         help for upgrade
      --keep-going[=true|false]   with --security: go on to the next server after a failure or an unexpected change
      --no-sudo[=true|false]      do not use sudo (like when logged in as root)
      --refresh[=true|false]      with --security: refresh the package index first
      --security[=true|false]     install only the security updates, one server at a time

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando policy edit --help
exit 0
--- stdout
--off switches a rule off, so it no longer stops a command. With
--add-server or --add-group it is off only on those servers (a group as its
servers are now): a command that also runs on another server is still
stopped. Switching a rule off weakens a safety check, so komando asks first:
an AI agent's request opens the approval window on your screen, and for a
rule that keeps the others working (check-failed, decode-run, rm-root, mkfs,
sshd-stop, ...) you type the rule's name at a terminal, with --yes too, and
an AI agent's request for one is refused. The audit log keeps every switch,
and `komando doctor` names every rule that is off. --off=false switches it
on again everywhere; --rm-server and --rm-group switch it on again on those
servers only.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; unless it only switches the
rule on: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

Usage:
  komando policy edit RULE [flags]

Examples:
  komando policy edit docker-prune --off --add-server build1
  komando policy edit docker-prune --off --add-server build1 --dry-run
  komando policy edit pkg-remove-essential --off --add-group lab
  komando policy edit docker-prune --rm-server build1
  komando policy edit docker-prune --off=false

Flags:
      --add-group strings    with --off: only on the servers in these groups as they are now
      --add-server strings   with --off: only on these servers
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for edit
      --off[=true|false]     switch the rule off; --off=false switches it on again everywhere
      --rm-group strings     switch the rule on again on the servers these groups named
      --rm-server strings    switch the rule on again on these servers

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando queue --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Read and send messages on Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SQS and Pub/Sub. Add a
queue with `komando queue add`.

info, ls, describe, peek, groups and lag only read: peek reads Kafka
messages without joining a consumer group, gives RabbitMQ and Pub/Sub
messages straight back, reads NATS stream messages by their number, and
receives SQS messages without hiding or deleting them, so nothing is
removed. send and create change (production queues ask first); rm and purge
delete messages, so they also need --allow-dangerous. Try any change with
--dry-run first. In RabbitMQ words a topic is a queue; in NATS words it is
a stream. Pub/Sub keeps messages in subscriptions: peek and purge take a
subscription, and groups lists them.

Usage:
  komando queue [flags]
  komando queue [command]

Aliases:
  queue, kafka, rabbitmq, nats, sqs, pubsub, queues

Examples:
  komando queue add prod-kafka kafka://10.0.0.8:9092 --via web1
  komando queue list prod-kafka
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders -n 5
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --value '{"id": 42}' --dry-run
  komando queue lag prod-kafka billing

Available Commands:
  add         Add a message queue
  create      Create a topic, queue or stream
  describe    One topic, queue or stream: messages, settings, and who reads it
  groups      List Kafka consumer groups, NATS consumers or Pub/Sub subscriptions
  info        Server summary: version, brokers or nodes, topic, queue or stream count
  lag         How far one Kafka consumer group (or NATS consumer) is behind
  list        List topics (or queues, or streams) with their message counts
  peek        Read the newest (or oldest) messages without removing any
  purge       Empty a topic, queue or stream and keep it
  rm          Delete topics, queues or streams with their messages
  send        Publish one message

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for queue

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando queue [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

Same as `komando conn add NAME URL`, for a message queue.

Flags:
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored in the vault as secret:NAME-pass and used as --password-ref
  -g, --group strings               put it in these groups (comma-separated)
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --login string                how komando logs in, as show names it: ask (a person types the password at every connect; never stored), password (a stored one: with --ask-password or --password-ref); a server also takes key (with --key or --identity) and agent (ssh-agent and ~/.ssh only), a conn none (no password of komando's own)
      --notes string                free-form notes (komando conn show shows them to people and agents)
      --option stringArray          an option of this kind, KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace a conn that has the same name
      --password-ref string         where the password is: secret:NAME (saved with komando secret set NAME), env:VAR, file:PATH or a password manager like op://...
      --protected[=true|false]      production: komando asks you before every change, and an AI agent needs your yes in a window
  -t, --tag strings                 tags, like prod (comma-separated)
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

### komando queue peek --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Kafka: read messages straight from the topic's partitions. No consumer
group is joined and no offset is committed, so no application notices and
nothing is removed. By default the newest -n messages over all partitions;
--oldest reads the first ones still kept.

RabbitMQ: take the first -n messages of the queue (the next ones a consumer
would get) and give them all back. Nothing is removed, but RabbitMQ marks
them redelivered, and a quorum queue counts each peek as a delivery: peek
stops (DELIVERY_LIMIT_NEAR) before a message runs out of them.

NATS: read messages straight from the stream by their sequence number. No
consumer is made and nothing is acknowledged, so nothing is removed, also
from a work-queue stream. The newest -n by default, --oldest for the first.

Amazon SQS: receive messages with a visibility timeout of 0 and never
delete them, so they stay and consumers can receive them at once. SQS gives
messages in no set order, so this is a sample of what waits. Every receive
counts toward a dead-letter queue's maxReceiveCount: peek stops
(DELIVERY_LIMIT_NEAR) before a message runs out of receives.

Google Cloud Pub/Sub: TOPIC is a subscription (messages wait there, not
in a topic). peek pulls messages without acknowledging them and gives them
straight back (ack deadline 0), so they stay and are delivered again at
once. With a dead-letter topic each pull counts as a delivery: peek stops
(DELIVERY_LIMIT_NEAR) before a message runs out of them.

Values that are not UTF-8 text are shown as base64.

Usage:
  komando queue peek CONN TOPIC [flags]

Examples:
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders -n 50 --partition 2
  komando queue peek prod-kafka orders --oldest -n 5

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]     help for peek
      --idle duration         Kafka: stop when no message came for this long (default 5s)
  -n, --limit int             how many messages (default 10)
      --oldest[=true|false]   the first messages still kept, not the newest
      --partition int         Kafka: only this partition, numbered from 0 (default: every partition)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando queue purge --help
