### komando queue send --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Publish one message to an existing topic (or queue) and wait until the
server keeps it. The value comes from --value, from a file (--from FILE;
'-' is stdin), or from data piped on stdin. --dry-run checks the topic and
the partition and sends nothing.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Kafka: --key picks the partition the usual way (the same key always goes
to the same partition); --partition picks one itself.
RabbitMQ: the message goes straight to the queue (the default exchange),
persistent, with --header values as its headers.
NATS: TOPIC is a subject that a stream keeps (orders.new); komando checks
which stream, publishes, and waits for the stream's acknowledgement.
Amazon SQS: text only; --header values become message attributes. A FIFO
queue (name.fifo) needs --key, the message group.
Google Cloud Pub/Sub: TOPIC is a topic; --header values become message
attributes and --key is the ordering key.

Usage:
  komando queue send CONN TOPIC [flags]

Examples:
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --value '{"id": 42, "status": "paid"}' --key 42
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --from ./order.json --header source=support
  komando queue send prod-kafka orders --value test --dry-run

Flags:
      --from string          read the message from this file ('-' for stdin)
      --header stringArray   a message header KEY=VALUE (repeatable)
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for send
      --key string           Kafka: the message key (picks the partition); SQS: the message group of a FIFO queue; Pub/Sub: the ordering key
      --partition int        Kafka: send to this partition, numbered from 0 (default: the broker's choice)
      --value string         the message

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando reboot --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Reboots each server in turn: komando asks it to reboot, waits until SSH
answers again, and checks that it started anew (a new boot id). The next
server is rebooted only when the one before came back; a server that does
not come back within --wait stops the rest.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

A reboot is a destructive action: it needs --allow-dangerous (and --yes or
the approval for protected servers). Try --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando reboot TARGET [flags]

Examples:
  komando reboot web1 --dry-run
  komando reboot @web --wait 10m --dry-run
  komando reboot @web --allow-dangerous --wait 10m   # after a person's yes

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for reboot
      --no-sudo[=true|false]   run without sudo
      --wait duration          how long each server may take to come back (like 10m, 1h) (default 5m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando registry --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Look at, copy and clean up container images. Add a registry with
`komando registry oci add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --ask-password`,
or bring in the ones you use with `komando import docker`.
ls and inspect only read, copy writes to the destination, rm and prune
delete images and need --allow-dangerous (try --dry-run first).

TLS options in the registry URL: ?ca=secret:NAME trusts a private CA (or
pins the registry's own certificate; the check stays on), ?tls=skip-verify
does not check the certificate, ?tls=false is plain HTTP. ?resolve=IP
connects to that IP instead of what DNS says (like curl --resolve). With
--via the last server looks the name up.

Usage:
  komando registry [flags]
  komando registry [command]

Aliases:
  registry, oci, registries

Examples:
  komando registry oci add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --ask-password
  komando registry oci image list ghcr myorg/api
  komando registry oci image show ghcr myorg/api:1.4.2
  komando registry oci image copy ghcr:myorg/api:1.4.2 harbor:prod/api:1.4.2
  komando registry oci image prune harbor prod/api --keep 10 --dry-run

Available Commands:
  oci         OCI registries: save them, and look after their images

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for registry

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando registry [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

### komando registry oci add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Save a oci registry under a short name.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when the address turns TLS
off (plain HTTP): it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

Usage:
  komando registry oci add NAME [URL] [flags]

Examples:
  komando registry oci add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --via web1
  komando registry oci add ghcr registry://myuser@ghcr.io --dry-run

Flags:
      --ask-password[=true|false]   type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored as a password credential
      --credential string           what it logs in with
      --group strings               put it in these groups
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --login string                how the password is used: ask at every connect, a stored one, or none
      --notes string                free-form notes, shown to people and agents
      --option stringArray          an option of this provider, KEY=VALUE (default [])
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace an entry that has the same name
      --protected[=true|false]      changes need a person's yes
      --tag strings                 tags, like prod
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:

Examples:

  komando registry oci remove ghcr

Flags:

  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv

  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando rename --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Without --starts-with: renames the one server, conn, VPN, secret, key or
group named OLD, as `komando host ssh rename` and the others do. When OLD
names two kinds of entry (a server and a secret), it says which commands to
use.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

With --starts-with: renames every server, conn, VPN, secret, key and group
whose name starts with OLD: OLD is replaced with NEW. When OLD ends in -,
the name OLD without it is renamed too (--starts-with shop- acme-shop- turns
group shop into acme-shop).

Every reference follows, as with `host rename` and `secret rename`: --via
paths, password, sudo, key, preshared key and passphrase references,
secret:NAME options in conn URLs, the key a server uses, group membership,
jobs and tunnels. A key komando made (key gen) lives in the sealed store, so
no file moves; a key file you added stays where it is. The protected mark,
labels, notes and creation time stay. Names inside URLs (a bucket, a
database user) are the resource's own and do not change.

--in-notes also replaces old names in notes, and --in-labels in label
values: server, conn, VPN and secret names as whole words, a group written
@NAME, and a pattern such as shop-db-* when it matches the same entries
after the rename. OLD without its -, group names without @, key names, and a
name that is also the user, host, bucket or database in a conn URL stay:
they often mean something else. The result lists each one it keeps ("kept"),
and each label value that names an old entry, with or without --in-labels.

Everything changes in one step, or nothing does: a new name that is taken
(or two old names that would get one new name) stops it before anything
is written. When NEW starts with OLD, names that start with NEW already
are left alone, so a second run changes nothing.

Renaming protected servers and conns needs --yes once, for all of them (an
AI agent's --yes opens one window for a person). See what would change with
--dry-run first. --kind renames only some kinds; references still follow. To
rename one entry, use host rename, conn rename, vpn rename, secret rename,
key rename or group rename.

Usage:
  komando rename OLD NEW [flags]

Examples:
  komando rename web1 web-01 --dry-run                 # one entry, whatever kind it is
  komando rename --starts-with shop- acme-shop- --dry-run   # the old -> new list and every reference
  komando rename --starts-with shop- acme-shop- --yes   # after a person's yes
  komando rename --starts-with old-registry registry --kind conn,secret
  komando rename --starts-with lab- test- --in-notes --in-labels --dry-run

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]          help for rename
      --in-labels[=true|false]     also replace old names in label values, as --in-notes does (label names stay)
      --in-notes[=true|false]      also replace old names in notes (server, conn, VPN and secret names, @group, OLD* patterns)
      --kind strings               rename only these kinds: host, conn, vpn, secret, key, group (default: all)
      --starts-with[=true|false]   rename every name that starts with OLD

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando safety --help
exit 0
--- stdout
How komando keeps a change from going wrong.

  --dry-run           every change can show what it would do first
  protected targets   a change asks [y/N] at your terminal; scripts and agents need --yes
  dangerous commands  rm -rf /, DROP DATABASE ...: you type the name; scripts need --allow-dangerous
  read only           db query, cache redis raw and cluster run only read unless you add --write
  audit               komando audit shows every change and who asked for it

An AI agent is never asked: it gets exit 6 and a person allows the flag in a
window on the screen. See docs/features/safety.md.

--- stderr

  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando secret --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Save a password once, then point to it as secret:NAME instead of typing it:
  komando secret set web1-pass
  komando host ssh edit web1 --password-ref secret:web1-pass

komando shows a saved value only to a person: at a terminal with
`secret show --reveal`, or after "Allow once" in komando's window; never
to an AI agent. `secret check` compares a value with the saved one
without showing either. `secret rename` and `secret cp` rename and copy.

How it is stored: each secret sealed with AES-256-GCM in
~/.komando/store.db. The random key is in the OS keychain (or in store.key
where there is none, or with KOMANDO_KEYCHAIN=off), or comes from
$KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS when that is set at first use (`secret passphrase`
changes it).

A --password-ref (and the other -ref flags) can also read a password your
team keeps elsewhere; komando reads it when needed and never stores it:
  env:VAR  file:PATH  vault:PATH#FIELD  aws-sm:NAME[#KEY]  gcp-sm:NAME[@PROJECT]
  azure-kv:VAULT/NAME[#KEY]  op://VAULT/ITEM/FIELD  bw://ITEM/FIELD  kdbx:FILE#GROUP/ENTRY

Usage:
  komando secret [flags]
  komando secret [command]

Aliases:
  secret, secrets, vault

Examples:
  komando secret set prod-db-pass                   # typed hidden
  komando secret list
  komando conn edit prod-db --password-ref secret:prod-db-pass
  komando secret rm old-pass --dry-run

Available Commands:
  check       Compare a typed value to a secret without showing either (person only)
  cp          Copy a secret to a new name in the vault (value never shown)
  keychain    Keep the vault key in the OS keychain instead of store.key
  list        List secret names, when they changed and what uses them
  passphrase  Change the vault passphrase and encrypt the secrets again (person only)
  rename      Rename a secret and every reference to it (value never shown)
  rm          Delete secrets for good
  run         Run a local command with vault secrets in its environment
  set         Store a secret, typed hidden or from a variable or a pipe
  show        Show that a secret exists, its value hidden

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for secret

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando secret [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando secret check --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Asks for a value (hidden, or from --from-env VAR or a pipe) and says whether
it is the stored one. When it is not, it says how they differ (only spaces
at the ends, only upper and lower case, or the number of characters), but
never shows either value.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

Only a person can run it: for an AI agent, a yes/no answer about a value it
picks would be a way to guess the secret one try at a time.

Usage:
  komando secret check NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando secret check vpn-pass            # type or paste it after the prompt
  pbpaste | komando secret check vpn-pass

Flags:
      --from-env string     read the value to compare from this environment variable
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for check

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando secret cp --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Stores the value of OLD under NEW as well. The value stays inside the vault:
it is never printed, so an AI agent can do this too. Nothing that uses OLD
changes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

When NEW exists already, --overwrite replaces its value; when a protected
server or conn uses NEW, that also needs --yes.

Usage:
  komando secret cp OLD NEW [flags]

Aliases:
  cp, copy

Examples:
  komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old
  komando secret cp db-pass db-pass-old --dry-run
  komando secret cp web-pass shared-pass --overwrite

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for cp
      --overwrite[=true|false]   replace NEW when it exists (what uses NEW then gets the value of OLD)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando secret keychain --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Moves the vault's key out of the store.key file into the operating system's
keychain, so a copy of ~/.komando (a backup, a synced folder) no longer
opens the vault or its secrets. The vault gets a new key as it moves, so a
copy of store.key made before opens nothing either, and the vault keeps
every secret. --off moves the key back into store.key, which needs --yes.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it turns the keychain
off: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); without --off: only
a person at a terminal can run it.

Only a person at a terminal moves the key in: the keychain may ask them to
unlock it, and an AI agent or a script cannot answer that.

Usage:
  komando secret keychain [flags]

Examples:
  komando secret keychain
  komando secret keychain --dry-run
  komando secret keychain --off --dry-run
  komando secret keychain --off --yes   # after a person's yes

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for keychain
      --off[=true|false]    move the key back into store.key (needs --yes)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando secret passphrase --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Re-encrypts every secret in the vault under a new passphrase, so you can
change KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS without losing your secrets. A vault whose key is
in store.key or in the OS keychain gets a passphrase this way, and the old
key is removed once the new vault is saved and read back.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

The vault is opened the usual way: with KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS, store.key or the
keychain. When KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS does not open a passphrase vault (you
changed it already, say), komando asks for the current passphrase. Then it
asks for the new one twice, hidden; it needs 15 or more characters. Every
secret is decrypted before anything is written: if one cannot be, nothing
changes.

Afterwards, put the new passphrase in KOMANDO_VAULT_PASS wherever you set it
(your shell profile, a password manager, a launch agent), and restart any
background tunnel or VPN session komando runs: they still hold the old key.

--off goes back to a new random key in store.key (needs --yes): a copy of
~/.komando then opens the vault again. `komando secret keychain` can move
that key into the OS keychain.

Only a person at a terminal can run it: an AI agent that chose the
passphrase, or put the key back in store.key, could open the vault on its
own. Anyone can preview it with --dry-run.

Usage:
  komando secret passphrase [flags]

Aliases:
  passphrase, passwd

Examples:
  komando secret passphrase               # asks for the new passphrase twice, hidden
  komando secret passphrase --dry-run
  komando secret passphrase --off --dry-run
  komando secret passphrase --off --yes   # after a person's yes

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for passphrase
      --off[=true|false]    back to a random key in store.key (needs --yes)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando secret rename --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Renames OLD to NEW inside the vault, and points every server, conn, key and
VPN that used secret:OLD at secret:NEW in the same step, so nothing stops
working and nobody types the value again. The value is never printed, so an

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)

### komando secret run --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Starts COMMAND on this computer with the --env values in its environment. A
value secret:NAME is read from the vault right before the program starts, so
it is never in the command line or the shell history. The program starts
directly, without a shell, with your environment minus komando's own
KOMANDO_* variables and the values that unlock the vault. For an AI agent
with secrets, --env may add variables but never replace one komando sets
(HOME, PATH, USER, LANG, ...), and may not set what decides which code or
settings the program loads: LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_*, NODE_OPTIONS, PYTHON*,
BASH_ENV, a pager, an editor, an askpass helper, an rc file, a proxy, GIT_*,
SSH_*, XDG_*, a tool's config file (KUBECONFIG, DOCKER_CONFIG,
*_CONFIG_FILE, AWS_*_FILE, NPM_CONFIG_*) or a toolchain's (CC, CXX, GOFLAGS,
GOTOOLCHAIN, CARGO_*, RUSTC_WRAPPER, JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_OPTS). The program
gets HOME, USER and LOGNAME from your OS account (USERPROFILE on Windows),
LANG, LC_*, TERM, TMPDIR, TZ, the Windows system folders, a system PATH and
its --env values.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when an AI agent hands a
saved secret to a program: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes
(--yes).

The program's output goes through komando's masking: a vault value it
prints shows as [secret:NAME]. komando exits with the program's exit code.

For an AI agent every secret:NAME needs a person's yes (--yes, then
komando's window names the secrets and the program), since the program
could print a value in a form masking does not know. A secret a protected
server, conn or VPN uses asks a person at a terminal too.

Usage:
  komando secret run -- COMMAND [ARGS...] [flags]

Examples:
  komando secret run --env PGPASSWORD=secret:db-main -- psql -h 10.0.0.5 -U app
  komando secret run -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=secret:aws-ci -e AWS_REGION=eu-west-1 -- terraform plan
  komando secret run --dry-run --env TOKEN=secret:gh-token -- ./deploy.sh

Flags:
  -e, --env stringArray     put KEY=VALUE or KEY=secret:NAME in the program's environment (repeatable)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for run

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando secret set --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Saves or replaces a password. Replacing one that a production server or
database uses asks first: it changes how komando logs in there. With --new
it only saves a new one: when NAME is in the vault already it stops with
SECRET_EXISTS and leaves the stored value alone.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

A value from a pipe loses the line breaks at its end (echo and pbpaste add
one). Spaces are kept, since a password can hold them; komando warns when
the value starts or ends with one, so a stray space copied with a password
is noticed. At the terminal, paste or type the value after the prompt
appears.

Usage:
  komando secret set NAME [flags]

Aliases:
  set, add

Examples:
  komando secret set web1-pass          # type or paste it after the prompt, nothing is shown
  komando secret set web1-pass --dry-run
  komando secret set db-pass --from-env DB_PASS
  pbpaste | komando secret set vpn-pass
  komando secret set api-token --new --from-env TOKEN   # never replaces one

Flags:
      --from-env string     read the value from this environment variable
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for set
      --new[=true|false]    only store a secret that is not in the vault yet; a taken NAME stops with SECRET_EXISTS

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando secret show --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Says whether the secret exists and what uses it, without its value. A person
at a terminal can add --reveal to print it; from a program without a
terminal (the Komando Mac app), komando first asks the person in its own
window. AI agents never get the value (they reference it as secret:NAME
instead). A warning says when the value starts or ends with a space, tab or
line break, a common cause of a failing login; 'komando secret check NAME'
lets a person compare it.

Usage:
  komando secret show NAME [flags]

Aliases:
  show, get

Examples:
  komando secret show db-pass
  komando secret show db-pass --reveal | pbcopy   # a person, at a terminal

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for show

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando ssh-gate --help
exit 0
--- stdout
ssh-gate lets an SSH key (a phone's, say) run komando on this computer, and
nothing else: no shell, no file copy, no port forwarding. Add the key to
~/.ssh/authorized_keys with the line `komando ssh-gate line` prints; sshd
then runs ssh-gate for it, whatever the key asks for.

Safety: only a person at a terminal can run it.

ssh-gate takes the command the key sent (SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND) only when it
is one komando command. It splits it into words like a shell, but expands
nothing and runs no shell: ; | & > < $ and backquotes are refused unless
they are quoted. One KOMANDO_AGENT=NAME may come before komando.

komando then runs as for an AI agent: secret values stay [hidden], --reveal
and --allow-dangerous are refused, and --yes for a protected server needs a
person on this computer. Commands that need a person at a terminal (shell,
db shell, secret passphrase ...) are refused (a --shell-access key may open
`komando host ssh shell SERVER`: see ssh-gate line; that shell is full
control of the server, outside these rules). The key runs commands on
servers, never one that writes on this computer or reads a file here (a
script, SQL or upload source by path; '-' for the key's own input works): no
download or cp to a file here (download --to - and cp SRC - stream to the
key's own output), no change to servers, VPNs, settings, rules, secrets,
keys or recipes in komando, no update, no change on a sqlite file or a
target at localhost or 127.x. With --read-only only commands that read run
(db query and cache redis raw without --write), and only those that stay on
the servers and conns in your list: no net, no cert check of a website, no
exec, job start, docker exec, cluster exec or recipe run, unless the line
also has --network. `komando ssh-gate status` tells a key which it is. Every
command a key runs or is refused is in `komando audit`, with --name, even
when the audit setting is off.

Usage:
  komando ssh-gate [flags]
  komando ssh-gate [command]

Examples:
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-read --read-only 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... phone'

Available Commands:
  line        Print the authorized_keys line that limits a key to komando
  status      Say which ssh-gate key runs this, and what it may do

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for ssh-gate

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando ssh-gate [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando ssh-gate line --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Prints the line to add to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on this computer, so the
key runs komando through ssh-gate and nothing else. PUBLIC_KEY is the key's
line (ssh-ed25519 AAAA... comment) or a .pub file holding it. The line names
this komando by its full path, as sshd does not search PATH.

A --read-only key runs only commands that read, and only those that stay
on the servers and conns in your list: no net checks, no cert check of
a website, and no exec, job start, docker exec, cluster exec or recipe run,
whose programs can connect anywhere and carry what they read in a URL or a
DNS name. Add --network too for a read key that may do those.

With --shell-access (not with --read-only) the key may also open a login
shell on one server: ssh -t HOST komando host ssh shell SERVER, word for
word. Its line has restrict,pty, so sshd gives it a terminal when it asks
for one. The shell is refused on a protected server, a Windows server or
this computer, with any other word or flag, without the terminal, and on
every server while you have deny rules of your own (komando policy list); db
shell and cluster shell stay refused. On the servers it opens on, the shell
is full control of the server, as the account komando logs in with: what is
typed is outside komando's per-command rules, masking and audit. Give such a
key only to a device you would give that login to. Each session's start and
end are in komando audit (key, server, how long, why it ended), and a
session with no input and no output for 30 minutes ends.

Usage:
  komando ssh-gate line PUBLIC_KEY --name NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-read --read-only 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... phone'
  komando ssh-gate line --name phone-checks --read-only --network ~/phone.pub
  komando ssh-gate line --name ops --shell-access ~/ops.pub

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for line
      --name string                 the key's name in the audit log (required)
      --network[=true|false]        with --read-only: the key may also run reads that reach the network (net, cert check of a URL, exec --read-only)
      --read-only[=true|false]      the key runs only commands that read
      --shell-access[=true|false]   the key may also open a login shell on one server (ssh -t HOST komando host ssh shell SERVER); not with --read-only

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

may do: change things, or read only, whether its reads may reach the

### komando status --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Lists what still runs after the command that started it ended: VPN sessions
(from vpn up, or started by a command), server logins kept by `komando login
SERVER`, AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) logins of the profiles in
~/.aws/config and when they end, tunnels, and the jobs started on servers.
Nothing is contacted, so it is quick and works offline. A job is listed
until `komando job rm`; whether it still runs is known on its server:
`komando job list --refresh` asks.

--short prints one line for your shell prompt: "vpn:1 tun:2" when one VPN
is up and two tunnels run, nothing when nothing runs. It reads only the
process numbers komando keeps beside its sealed store (no names, no key),
prints no JSON and never fails, so it is safe to run on every prompt.

zsh (also with oh-my-zsh), in ~/.zshrc:
  setopt PROMPT_SUBST
  RPROMPT='$(komando status --short)'

bash, in ~/.bashrc:
  PS1='$(p=$(komando status --short); [ -n "$p" ] && echo "[$p] ")'"$PS1"

starship, in ~/.config/starship.toml:
  [custom.komando]
  command = "komando status --short"
  when = true

Usage:
  komando status [flags]

Examples:
  komando status
  komando status -o json
  komando status --short   # prints for example vpn:2 tun:1, or nothing

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]    help for status
      --short[=true|false]   one line for your shell prompt, like vpn:1 tun:2 (no JSON, never fails)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando storage --help
exit 0
--- stdout
List, copy and share files in a bucket or on a file server. Add one with
`komando storage add`.

It works with an S3-compatible, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob bucket,
or a folder on a WebDAV, FTPS, FTP or SFTP server or an SMB share (Windows,
Samba, Azure Files). Keys are relative to the folder in the storage URL; a
key ending in / is a folder. ls, cat and download only read. upload,
mkdir, mv and chmod (SFTP only) change files and link shares one (S3,
Google Cloud and Azure; on production storage they ask first); rm deletes,
so it also needs --allow-dangerous.
Downloads never overwrite a local file unless --overwrite, and uploads to
file servers go to a temporary name first, so a failed upload leaves
nothing half written.

The storage itself: komando storage add, komando test CONN, komando conn
edit CONN, komando conn rm CONN. komando list kind:storage lists them.

Usage:
  komando storage [flags]
  komando storage [command]

Aliases:
  storage, s3

Examples:
  komando storage add backups 's3://AKIAEXAMPLE@my-bucket/db?region=eu-west-1' --ask-password
  komando storage list backups 2026/
  komando download backups 2026/app.sql.gz --to ./
  komando storage rm backups --prefix daily/ --older-than 30d --dry-run

Available Commands:
  add         Add a file storage
  cat         Show the text of an object
  chmod       Change the mode of a file or folder on an SFTP conn
  download    Download an object from a storage conn
  link        Make a temporary download link that works without a login
  list        List the objects and folders of a storage conn
  mkdir       Create a folder in a storage conn, with any missing parents
  mv          Move or rename a file or folder inside a storage conn
  rm          Delete objects by name or prefix
  upload      Upload a file to a storage conn

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for storage

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando storage [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr

exit 0

Same as `komando conn add NAME URL`, for a file storage.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Saves a file storage under a short name. Typed alone at a terminal, it asks
step by step. The URL scheme sets the kind: `komando conn kinds` lists them.

Usage:
  komando storage add NAME URL [flags]

Examples:
  komando storage add backups 's3://AKIAEXAMPLE@my-bucket/db?region=eu-west-1' --ask-password
  komando storage add backups 's3://AKIAEXAMPLE@my-bucket/db?region=eu-west-1' --ask-password --dry-run

  komando storage add site 'sftp://deploy@files.example.com/uploads'

  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for add
      --label stringArray           label KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --login string                how komando logs in, as show names it: ask (a person types the password at every connect; never stored), password (a stored one: with --ask-password or --password-ref); a server also takes key (with --key or --identity) and agent (ssh-agent and ~/.ssh only), a conn none (no password of komando's own)
      --notes string                free-form notes (komando conn show shows them to people and agents)
      --option stringArray          an option of this kind, KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --overwrite[=true|false]      replace a conn that has the same name
      --password-ref string         where the password is: secret:NAME (saved with komando secret set NAME), env:VAR, file:PATH or a password manager like op://...
      --protected[=true|false]      production: komando asks you before every change, and an AI agent needs your yes in a window
  -t, --tag strings                 tags, like prod (comma-separated)
      --via string                  reach it through these servers (bastions) or a VPN first, comma-separated path; no local port is opened

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or

exit 0
--- stdout
Sets the Unix mode of PATH (a file or a folder) on an SFTP server, like
chmod. MODE is in digits: 0644, 640, 0750, or 2775 with the setgid bit; the
result says the old mode too. Only SFTP servers have modes: other kinds of
storage stop with STORAGE_UNSUPPORTED before anything is contacted.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

### komando storage link --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Prints a URL anyone can use to download KEY until it expires (default 1
hour, at most 7 days). Treat it like a password while it is valid. Sharing
from a protected conn needs --yes. An AI agent gets a link only when a
person allows --reveal, and never for a file that is a secret by its name
(.env, a key): a link is the file as it is, past the hiding of storage cat
and download. The link itself is not stored in the audit log. The link names
the storage address in the conn URL: when komando reaches it through --via,
only people who can reach that address can use the link. --endpoint signs
the link for the address they use instead (S3 only).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when an AI agent makes a link
(a person allows --reveal): it weakens a safety check: a person's yes
(--yes); on a protected server or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando storage link CONN OBJECT [flags]

Aliases:
  link, presign, share

Examples:
  komando storage link backups reports/q3.pdf --expires 24h
  komando storage link backups reports/q3.pdf --expires 24h --dry-run
  komando storage link backups reports/q3.pdf --expires 7d
  komando storage link backups reports/q3.pdf --endpoint https://files.example.com

Flags:
      --endpoint string     sign the link for this address, like https://files.example.com (when komando reaches the storage through --via)
      --expires duration    how long the link works, like 30m, 24h or 7d (at most 7d) (default 1h)
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for link

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

exit 0

Makes the folder PATH and any missing folders above it. A folder that is
already there is fine (created: false); a file with that name stops it
(FILE_EXISTS).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or

### komando storage mv --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Moves SRC to DST inside one conn. A DST ending in / is a folder: SRC moves
into it and keeps its name. Missing folders above DST are made. A file
already at DST stops the move (FILE_EXISTS) unless --overwrite; a folder
at DST is never replaced.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

On a file server (SFTP, FTP, FTPS, WebDAV, SMB) mv is one rename on the
server, and moves folders too.

S3, Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob cannot rename: mv copies the object
on the server, checks that the copy has the same size and checksum, and
only then deletes the original (method: copy_then_delete). If the check
fails, the original stays and the copy is deleted (MOVE_FAILED). There
mv moves one object at a time, not a folder. In a bucket that keeps old
versions, the original's old versions stay.

Usage:
  komando storage mv CONN SRC DST [flags]

Examples:
  komando storage mv backups db/old.sql.gz archive/ --dry-run
  komando storage mv backups db/old.sql.gz archive/
  komando storage mv backups reports/draft.pdf reports/q3.pdf --overwrite

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for mv
      --overwrite[=true|false]   replace a file already at DST (never a folder)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando storage rm --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Without --prefix, rm takes exact keys (no patterns). With --prefix it
removes every object under that folder, or with --older-than only the ones
older than that (30d, 12h): the usual cleanup of old backups. --dry-run
lists them first; --max-remove (default 1000) refuses to go on when more
would be removed.

Safety: dangerous, it cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on,
and an AI agent or a script needs --allow-dangerous; on a protected server
or conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

In an S3 bucket with versioning, rm leaves the old versions behind (and a
delete marker): --all-versions removes every version of the keys too, so
they are really gone. `storage list CONN PREFIX --all-versions` shows them.

Usage:
  komando storage rm CONN [OBJECT...] [flags]

Aliases:
  rm, remove, delete, del

Examples:
  komando storage rm backups tmp/old.sql.gz --dry-run
  komando storage rm backups tmp/old.sql.gz --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando storage rm backups --prefix daily/ --older-than 30d --dry-run
  komando storage rm backups --prefix daily/ --older-than 30d --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes

Flags:
      --all-versions[=true|false]   S3: also remove every old version and delete marker of the keys, so they are really gone
  -h, --help[=true|false]           help for rm
      --max-remove int              refuse when more than this many objects would be removed (default 1000)
      --older-than duration         with --prefix: only objects older than this (like 30d, 12h, 90m)
      --prefix string               remove everything under this folder (like daily/; / for the whole conn)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando storage upload --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Same as `komando upload TARGET FILE [DEST]`.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

Usage:
  komando storage upload CONN FILE [OBJECT] [flags]

Aliases:
  upload, put

Examples:
  komando storage upload backups ./report.pdf reports/2026/
  komando storage upload backups ./report.pdf reports/2026/ --dry-run

Flags:
      --continue[=true|false]    go on with a copy that was cut off: keep the part already at the destination when it matches the source, send the rest, then check the whole file (sha256)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for upload
      --progress[=true|false]    with -o json, write progress to the error output (stderr), one JSON object per line
  -r, --recursive[=true|false]   upload a folder (new and changed files, like komando sync)
      --size bytes               an upload from stdin (-): how many bytes it sends, like 10MiB; a stream of another length replaces nothing (SIZE_CONFLICT)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

  reload        Reload units (sudo) and report the resulting state
  restart       Restart units (sudo) and report the resulting state
  start         Start units (sudo) and report the resulting state

  stop          Stop units (sudo) and report the resulting state

### komando sync --help
exit 0
--- stdout
One side is a folder on this computer; the other is TARGET:PATH on servers
(many at once: @web:/var/www/site) or CONN:PREFIX in a storage conn (a
bucket or a file server). Files that are new, a different size or file mode,
or newer in SRC are copied; the rest are left alone. --delete also removes
files SRC no longer has (that needs --allow-dangerous). --exclude skips
names or paths (shell globs, repeatable). Try --dry-run first: it lists
every file it would touch.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --delete: dangerous, it
cannot be undone: a person types the name to go on, and an AI agent or a
script needs --allow-dangerous.

--delete stops before it empties a folder that SRC lists as empty while
DST has files in it: a listing cut short looks like that. A person types
the folder to go on; a script names each folder it means with --emptied
(--allow-dangerous alone does not do), or removes the folder on DST first.

--sudo writes on the servers as root, for a folder the SSH user cannot
write (/etc/nginx): each file goes in as `upload --sudo` puts one, staged
privately and checked by root, keeping the owner of a file that is there;
the SSH user still needs to read the folder.

Usage:
  komando sync SRC DST [flags]

Examples:
  komando sync ./site @web:/var/www/site --exclude .git --dry-run
  komando sync ./site web1:/var/www/site --delete --dry-run
  komando sync ./site web1:/var/www/site --delete --allow-dangerous   # after a person's yes
  komando sync ./nginx @web:/etc/nginx/conf.d --sudo --dry-run
  komando sync ./backups backups:2026/ --exclude '*.tmp'
  komando sync backups:2026/ ./restore
  komando sync web1:/var/log/app ./logs/web1

Flags:
      --delete[=true|false]     also remove files that SRC does not have (needs --allow-dangerous)
      --emptied stringArray     with --delete: this folder of SRC is empty on purpose, so its files go from DST (repeatable)
      --exclude stringArray     skip names or paths matching this glob (repeatable), like .git, '*.log'
  -h, --help[=true|false]       help for sync
      --progress[=true|false]   with -o json, write progress to the error output (stderr), one JSON object per line
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]       write on the servers as root, file by file as upload --sudo does (a folder here to servers)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando test --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Logs in to each server (and checks who it is and whether sudo needs a
password), connects to each conn and checks each VPN.

--wait 5m waits for new servers: komando tests again every few seconds until
every target passes or the time is up, for example right after a cloud
server was created or rebuilt. It does not wait out a changed host key
(HOSTKEY_MISMATCH), a refused login (AUTH_FAILED: retrying could get your
address banned), a VPN that needs a login, or a local key or secret problem:
those fail at once. To wait for the server's own start-up too, run `komando
host ssh exec TARGET --read-only -- cloud-init status --wait` next.

A server that asks for a password or a two-factor code only a person can
answer: when a person runs test at a terminal, komando asks once and keeps
the session open for the login_for setting (8 hours). An AI agent's commands
to that server reuse the session; when it has expired they fail and name
this command, and an agent never types a code. --end closes the kept session
of the servers it names, or of every server when it names none; `komando
status` lists the kept sessions.

Usage:
  komando test TARGET [flags]

Aliases:
  test, ping

Examples:
  komando test @prod
  komando test all
  komando test @new --wait 5m   # right after creating servers
  komando test --end            # end every kept session

Flags:
      --end[=true|false]    end the kept sessions of the servers named (every server when none is named), instead of testing
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for test
      --wait duration       test again every few seconds until every target passes, for up to this long (like 5m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando update --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Replaces this komando program with the newest release from GitHub, or with
the VERSION you name. It checks that the release is signed with the komando
project's key (a release without that signature is refused), checks the
download against the release's signed checksums.txt, and tries the new
program before it replaces the old one. If anything fails, the old komando
stays as it was.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; when it installs an older
version: it weakens a safety check: a person's yes (--yes).

See whether there is a newer version, changing nothing: komando update
--dry-run.

komando lives in a folder only root may change (/usr/local/bin, for
example)? Then run it with sudo: sudo komando update. As root it writes
nothing in ~/.komando; otherwise the update goes into the audit log like
other changes.

Going back to an older version needs a person's yes (--yes for an agent): an
older komando may lack safety checks this one has. Without a VERSION it
never goes back.

A komando built from source that is not a release (make build, or go build
of a commit between releases) is not replaced: build it again instead. One
that reports a release version (go install ...@v0.12.0, or go build at a
release tag) counts as that release and is replaced. --timeout limits the
whole update (default 10m).

Usage:
  komando update [VERSION] [flags]

Examples:
  komando update --dry-run    # is there a newer version?
  komando update              # install the newest release
  sudo komando update         # komando is in /usr/local/bin
  komando update v0.14.0      # install this version

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for update

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando upload --help
exit 0
--- stdout
DEST is the path on the servers, or the key in the storage conn. It defaults
to the file's name (servers: in the login user's home folder; ~/x works
too). A storage KEY ending in / is a folder, so the file keeps its name
inside it. An existing file at DEST is replaced (the result says replaced).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; on a protected server or
conn, a person's yes (--yes) as well.

FILE - reads the file from stdin into DEST, which then names the file: on a
server through a temporary file moved into place at the end. --size N
makes a stream of another length fail (SIZE_CONFLICT) and replace nothing.

--continue goes on with an upload of one file that was cut off: the part
already at DEST is kept when it matches the file (sha256), the rest is
sent, and the whole file is checked. S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure
Blob and WebDAV store a file whole and cannot add to one
(RESUME_UNSUPPORTED).

Folders (-r), like cp and rsync:
  FILE/  (trailing slash)  the contents of FILE go into DEST
  FILE   into a new DEST    DEST becomes the copy of FILE
  FILE   into a folder DEST of the same name (site -> /var/www/site): DEST
         is updated in place, so running the same upload again never nests
         site/site
  FILE   into another existing folder DEST: the copy is DEST/FILE
Without DEST the folder keeps its name (servers: in the home folder). In
storage, a DEST ending in / is an existing folder. Symbolic links are not
copied (they are listed as skipped). For repeatable deploys that send only
changed files, use `komando sync`.

Usage:
  komando upload TARGET FILE [DEST] [flags]

Examples:
  komando upload @web ./app.tar.gz /tmp/app.tar.gz
  komando upload @web ./app.tar.gz /tmp/app.tar.gz --dry-run
  komando upload web1 ./site /var/www/site -r
  komando upload web1 ./nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf --sudo
  komando upload backups ./db.sql.gz 2026/db.sql.gz
  komando upload web1 ./db.sql.gz /var/backups/db.sql.gz --continue
  komando upload web1 - /etc/app/motd --size 120 < motd.txt

Flags:
      --continue[=true|false]    go on with a copy that was cut off: keep the part already at the destination when it matches the source, send the rest, then check the whole file (sha256)
  -h, --help[=true|false]        help for upload
      --mode string              file mode, like 0755
  -p, --parents[=true|false]     create missing parent folders
      --progress[=true|false]    with -o json, write progress to the error output (stderr), one JSON object per line
  -r, --recursive[=true|false]   copy folders (a trailing / on SRC copies its contents)
      --size bytes               an upload from stdin (-): how many bytes it sends, like 10MiB; a stream of another length replaces nothing (SIZE_CONFLICT)
  -s, --sudo[=true|false]        install into place with sudo (single files)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando user --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Linux user accounts: see, add, lock, remove

Usage:
  komando user [flags]
  komando user [command]

Aliases:

Examples:

  komando user add web1 alice --key alice --admin
  komando user lock web1 alice                      # keep the account, stop logins
  komando user rm web1 alice --remove-home --dry-run

Available Commands:
  add         Create a user if missing, with an SSH key and sudo if asked
  list        List accounts with admin group and lock state (--all for system)
  lock        Lock an account so password and SSH keys stop working
  rm          Delete a user account
  unlock      Unlock an account locked with `user lock`

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for user
      --no-sudo[=true|false]   do not use sudo (like when logged in as root)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando user [command] --help" for more information about a command.

### komando user list --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Lists accounts with their uid, home, shell, whether they are in the sudo,
wheel or admin group (admin_group; rules in sudoers.d are not read) and
whether the account is locked (expired, as `komando user lock` does). The
lock state is read through sudo; with --no-sudo it is left out.

Usage:
  komando user list TARGET [flags]

Aliases:
  list, ls

Examples:
  komando user list web1

Flags:
  -a, --all[=true|false]       include system accounts
  -h, --help[=true|false]      help for list
  -n, --limit int              show at most this many accounts per server (0 = all)
      --no-sudo[=true|false]   do not use sudo (like when logged in as root)

### komando vpn --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Add a VPN once, then put it first in --via. A command that needs it
connects it, using the login you saved:

  komando vpn add office wireguard --config ~/Downloads/office.conf
  komando vpn add client-x globalprotect --portal vpn.client.com --user alice --password-ref secret:client-x --mfa
  komando host ssh add app admin@10.0.0.5 --via office,bastion
  komando host ssh exec app -- uptime

VPNs with --mfa need a person: run `komando vpn up NAME` once and later
commands (and agents) reuse that session. komando never answers MFA.

Kinds (also: pritunl = openvpn; cisco, xauth = ipsec):
  anyconnect    Cisco AnyConnect / ocserv, run inside komando (no openconnect)
  f5            F5 BIG-IP SSL VPN
  fortinet      Fortinet SSL VPN (FortiClient)
  globalprotect Palo Alto GlobalProtect
  ikev2         IKEv2/IPsec (pre-shared key or EAP login with a server certificate), run inside komando
  ipsec         Cisco-style IPsec (IKEv1, group name and XAUTH login), run inside komando
  l2tp          L2TP/IPsec with a pre-shared key, run inside komando (no admin rights)
  openvpn       OpenVPN, also Pritunl profiles, run inside komando (no openvpn program, Docker or admin rights)
  proxy         an HTTP proxy (CONNECT), such as a company proxy: every connection is tunneled through it
  pulse         Pulse Secure / Ivanti Connect Secure
  socks         a SOCKS5 proxy that is already running (`komando host ssh tunnel start TARGET -D`, a company proxy)
  system        a VPN set up in your computer's settings; --service lets `vpn up` connect it
  tailscale     Tailscale or Headscale, run inside komando (no tailscaled, no admin rights)
  wireguard     WireGuard, run inside komando (no admin rights, many at once)

Usage:
  komando vpn [flags]
  komando vpn [command]

Aliases:
  vpn, vpns

Examples:
  komando vpn add office wireguard --config ~/Downloads/office.conf
  komando vpn test office
  komando host ssh edit db1 --via office --dry-run
  komando vpn up office

Available Commands:
  add         Add a VPN
  down        Disconnect VPN sessions (--all for every one)
  edit        Change one or more VPNs (only the flags you pass change)
  list        List VPNs
  rename      Rename a VPN and every reference to it
  rm          Remove VPNs (from komando only)
  show        Show a VPN (saved keys are never shown)
  status      Which VPNs are connected, since when, and what uses them
  test        Check that VPNs connect
  up          Connect a VPN now and keep it up

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for vpn

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

Use "komando vpn [command] --help" for more information about a command.
--- stderr
### komando vpn add --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Saves a VPN under a short name. Typed alone at a terminal, it asks step by
step, starting with the VPN app your company uses.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Which flags go with which VPN kind:
  every kind     takes --check, --mfa, --protected, --label, -g, -t,
                 --notes, --overwrite
  wireguard      needs --config (the .conf file)
  openvpn        needs --config (the .ovpn file) and --check; takes --user,
                 --password-ref, --ask-password
  globalprotect, needs --portal (the VPN server or portal); takes --user,
  fortinet,      --password-ref, --ask-password
  anyconnect,
  pulse, f5
  l2tp           needs --server, --user and --psk-ref or --ask-psk; takes
                 --password-ref, --ask-password, --legacy-crypto,
                 --allow-pap
  ipsec          needs --server and --psk-ref (the group password) or
                 --ask-psk; takes --id (the group name), --user,
                 --password-ref, --ask-password, --legacy-crypto
  ikev2          needs --server and --psk-ref, --ask-psk or --user; takes
                 --password-ref, --ask-password, --id (your identity),
                 --remote-id (the server's identity), --ca (the server's CA,
                 PEM)
  tailscale      takes --password-ref (the auth key), --server (a Headscale
                 login server)
  system         needs --check; takes --service (its name in your computer's
                 settings)
  socks, proxy   needs --proxy-address; takes --user, --password-ref,
                 --ask-password

Usage:
  komando vpn add NAME KIND [flags]

Examples:
  komando vpn add office wireguard --config ~/Downloads/office.conf --check 10.0.0.5:22
  komando vpn add office wireguard --config ~/Downloads/office.conf --check 10.0.0.5:22 --dry-run
  komando vpn add client-x globalprotect --portal vpn.client.com   # signs in through a browser window at vpn up
  komando vpn add office openvpn --config office.ovpn --user alice --password-ref secret:office --check 10.8.0.1:22
  komando vpn add tailnet tailscale --password-ref secret:ts-authkey
  komando vpn add office l2tp --server vpn.example.com --psk-ref secret:office-psk --user alice --ask-password   # type the password now (hidden)
  komando vpn add old-office l2tp --server vpn.example.com --psk-ref secret:old-psk --user alice --legacy-crypto --allow-pap
  komando vpn add asa ipsec --server asa.client.com --id staff --psk-ref secret:asa-group --user alice
  komando vpn add cloud ikev2 --server vpn.example.com --user alice --password-ref secret:cloud
  komando vpn add corp system --service "Corp VPN" --check 10.20.0.1:443
  komando vpn add lab socks --proxy-address 127.0.0.1:1080
  komando vpn add office proxy --proxy-address proxy.corp.example:3128   # a company HTTP proxy

Flags:
      --allow-pap[=true|false]       L2TP: let the server pick a login that does not prove it is the server: PAP, which hands it your password itself, CHAP-MD5 or none (needs a person's yes)
      --ask-password[=true|false]    type the password now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored in the vault as secret:NAME-pass and used as --password-ref
      --ask-psk[=true|false]         L2TP, IPsec, IKEv2: type the pre-shared key now (hidden, a person at a terminal); it is stored in the vault as secret:NAME-psk and used as --psk-ref
      --ca string                    IKEv2: the CA certificate (PEM) that signed the server's certificate, if not a public one
      --check string                 host:port reachable only through this VPN (vpn up and test connect to it; needed for system and openvpn)
      --config string                WireGuard: the .conf file; OpenVPN: the .ovpn file (both kept in the vault)
  -g, --group strings                put it in these groups (comma-separated)
  -h, --help[=true|false]            help for add
      --id string                    IPsec: the group name; IKEv2: your identity (default: --user, or your address)
      --label stringArray            label KEY=VALUE (repeatable) (default [])
      --legacy-crypto[=true|false]   L2TP, IPsec: also offer 3DES and DH groups 2 and 5, for old servers (weak; needs a person's yes)
      --mfa[=true|false]             the login needs a person (MFA, SSO): only 'vpn up' run by a person connects it
      --notes string                 free-form notes
      --overwrite[=true|false]       replace a VPN with the same name
      --password-ref string          where the password is (Tailscale: the auth key): secret:NAME (saved with komando secret set NAME), env:VAR, file:PATH or a password manager like op://...
      --portal string                GlobalProtect, Fortinet, AnyConnect, Pulse, F5: the VPN server or portal
      --protected[=true|false]       komando asks a person before it changes or removes this VPN; an AI agent needs their yes in a window
      --proxy-address string         SOCKS: host:port of the proxy; proxy: host:port or http(s)://host:port
      --psk-ref string               L2TP, IPsec, IKEv2: the pre-shared key (IPsec: the group password), as a reference like --password-ref
      --remote-id string             IKEv2: the server's identity, if not its --server name
      --server string                L2TP, IPsec, IKEv2: the VPN server (host or host:port); Tailscale: a Headscale login server URL
      --service string               System VPN: its name in your computer's settings, so 'vpn up' can connect it
  -t, --tag strings                  tags, like prod (comma-separated)
      --user string                  user name for the VPN login

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

### komando vpn edit --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Changes the common settings of a VPN. To give a WireGuard or OpenVPN VPN a
new config file, add it again with --overwrite. -g and -t add a group or a
tag, as in host edit; --rm-group and --rm-tag take one away. Give several
names or a selector (@group, tag:office) to change many VPNs at once.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first; with --mfa=false: it weakens
a safety check: a person's yes (--yes); with --protected=false: it weakens a
safety check: a person's yes (--yes); on a protected server or conn, a
person's yes (--yes) as well.

--protected marks a VPN komando asks a person about before it is changed
or removed. Turning that off, or turning --mfa off, needs a person's yes.

Usage:
  komando vpn edit TARGET... [flags]

Examples:
  komando vpn edit office --check 10.0.0.5:22
  komando vpn edit lab --proxy-address 127.0.0.1:1081
  komando vpn edit client-x --password-ref secret:client-x-new
  komando vpn edit office --server vpn2.example.com --psk-ref secret:office-psk-2
  komando vpn edit client-x --portal gw2.client.com
  komando vpn edit office -g jakarta --rm-group old --label site=jkt
  komando vpn edit @office --protected --dry-run

Flags:
      --add-group strings            put it in these groups (comma-separated)
      --add-tag strings              add these tags (comma-separated)
      --allow-pap[=true|false]       L2TP: let the server pick a login that does not prove it is the server: PAP, which hands it your password itself, CHAP-MD5 or none (turning it on needs a person's yes)
      --ca string                    IKEv2: the CA certificate (PEM) that signed the server's certificate; "" for a public one
      --check string                 host:port reachable only through this VPN
  -h, --help[=true|false]            help for edit
      --id string                    IPsec: the group name; IKEv2: your identity
      --label stringArray            set label KEY=VALUE (an empty value removes it) (default [])
      --legacy-crypto[=true|false]   L2TP, IPsec: also offer 3DES and DH groups 2 and 5, for old servers (weak; turning it on needs a person's yes)
      --mfa[=true|false]             the login needs a person (MFA, SSO)
      --notes string                 free-form notes
      --password-ref string          password as secret:NAME | env:VAR | file:PATH | op://... | bw://... | kdbx:... | vault:PATH#FIELD | aws-sm:NAME | gcp-sm:NAME | azure-kv:VAULT/NAME
      --portal string                GlobalProtect, Fortinet, AnyConnect, Pulse, F5: the VPN server or portal
      --protected[=true|false]       komando asks a person before it changes or removes this VPN; an AI agent needs their yes in a window
      --proxy-address string         SOCKS: host:port of the proxy; proxy: host:port or http(s)://host:port
      --psk-ref string               L2TP, IPsec, IKEv2: the pre-shared key (IPsec: the group password)
      --remote-id string             IKEv2: the server's identity
      --rm-group strings             take it out of these groups
      --rm-tag strings               remove these tags
      --server string                L2TP, IPsec, IKEv2: the VPN server
      --service string               System VPN: its name in your computer's settings
      --unset strings                clear these settings: user,password-ref,psk-ref,id,remote-id,ca,check,notes
      --user string                  user name for the VPN login

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando vpn rename --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Gives a VPN a new name. Its settings stay, and every --via path that starts
with it follows the new name. The vault secrets `vpn add` made under its
name (NAME-key, NAME-config, ...) move to the new name when only this VPN
uses them, so the old name is free again. Disconnect it first (`komando vpn
down NAME`) if it is up.

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando vpn rename OLD NEW [flags]

Aliases:
  rename, mv

Examples:
  komando vpn rename office office-jkt
  komando vpn rename office office-jkt --dry-run

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for rename

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)

### komando vpn status --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Shows each VPN with up yes/no. Session VPNs are up while their session
runs; a SOCKS proxy is up when its address answers, a system VPN when its
--check address answers. WireGuard connects for each command.

Usage:
  komando vpn status [flags]

Examples:
  komando vpn status

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for status

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr
### komando vpn test --help
exit 0
--- stdout
Same as `komando test`.

Usage:
  komando vpn test TARGET [flags]

Aliases:
  test, ping

Examples:
  komando vpn test office

Flags:
      --end[=true|false]    end the kept sessions of the servers named (every server when none is named), instead of testing
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for test
      --wait duration       test again every few seconds until every target passes, for up to this long (like 5m)

Global Flags (all of them: komando --help):
      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing
  -o, --output string          json or text (default $KOMANDO_OUTPUT, or
                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
                               takes csv and tsv
      --timeout duration       time limit per server, like 30s or 1h (default: setting default_timeout, 5m)
  -y, --yes[=true|false]       confirm a change on a protected target (an AI agent needs a person's yes)
--- stderr

exit 0
--- stdout
Connect a VPN now and keep it up for later commands (a person logs in here,
MFA included).

Safety: a change; try it with --dry-run first.

Usage:
  komando vpn up NAME [flags]

Examples:
  komando vpn up office
  komando vpn up office --dry-run

Flags:
  -h, --help[=true|false]   help for up

      --dry-run[=true|false]   show what would run, changing nothing

                               text in a terminal, JSON when piped); db query also
